# Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability

Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation

Ajay Pravin Mahale, 12 August 2026

###### Abstract

Does circuit-discovery evidence, filed as EU AI Act technical documentation, survive two competent analysts using the same system and tool with different defensible settings? We pre-registered a crossed grid of seven analytic axes, all levels from published implementations, and mapped each circuit deterministically to a structured Annex IV statement. On GPT-2 small and IOI, 7,561 of 15,840 specifications produced a claim. Claims fail filability at every plausible tolerance, even with the metric standardised or circuit size removed and fixed. Circuits are near-disjoint and functionally uncorrelated. One of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library's canonical task. One model, one task; scale untested.

## 1 Introduction

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (consolidated, amended by 2026/1744, CELEX 02024R1689-20260727, read 11 Aug 2026): Annex IV 2(b) asks for "the general logic of the AI system and of the algorithms"; 2(e) for "an assessment of the technical measures needed to facilitate the interpretation of the outputs"; Art. 86(1) grants "clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken". A filed circuit account has value only if a second analyst would file something compatible. We propose no better method and do not call interpretability worthless.

Contributions: (i) pre-registered seven-axis multiverse plus deterministic circuit→Annex IV map; (ii) filability criterion $\pi^{*}\geq 1-\alpha$, measured on a canonical task; (iii) instability survives standardising any one axis and removing/fixing size; (iv) pooled multiverse statistics can invert when specifications select different-sized objects; three of ours do.

## 2 Related work

- Non-identifiability: Méloux et al. show a unique explanation need not exist; we measure its cost when filed.
- Faithfulness metric sensitivity: Miller et al. find scores highly sensitive to minor choices (one axis); we cross seven and use their library, stress-testing the tooling by its own definitions.
- Structure vs. function: Bayat Makou et al. find structurally distinct circuits computing the same thing ("phantom specialisation"), the strongest objection: a flip rate might only measure which equivalent member was sampled. Section 7.6 answers functionally: our circuits are not interchangeable.
- Variance as estimation: Méloux et al.; seed is one of our axes.
- Auditability: Lan et al. call for auditing standards; we give a measurement and criterion. Sharkey et al. list open problems; Mueller et al. argue for standardised evaluation.
- Multiverse method: Steegen et al.; specification curve of Simonsohn et al.; Simmons et al. on analytic flexibility, which can manufacture a stability claim.
- Hsia et al.: sufficiency and comprehensiveness, two of our four metrics, can be inflated without changing predictions or explanations; hence per-metric discard rates.

## 3 What this paper is not claiming

- Not that circuits are no better than random: at fixed size, 0.2746 vs. size-matched null 0.4230.
- Not that mechanisms agree: functional instability 0.3972 pooled, 0.4777 at the smallest circuits.
- Not one mechanism differently described: kappa 0.0146.
- Not seed nondeterminism: the seed selects sampled prompts.
- Nothing about scale.

## 4 Formalism

Specification $s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)$: objective, ablation, corruption, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, granularity. Discovery returns $C(s)\subseteq E$; GPT-2 small, factorised q/k/v graph: $|E|=32{,}491$, confirmed by instrument and closed form (block $b$ attention gets $1+13b$ sources × 3 slots × 12 heads; MLP $b$ those plus own heads; output all 157 non-terminal sources). 156 components (144 heads, 12 MLPs).

$$D(s_{i},s_{j})=1-\frac{|C_{i}\cap C_{j}|}{|C_{i}\cup C_{j}|}\quad(1)$$
$\bar{J}$: mean pairwise Jaccard. For claim map $\varphi$:
$$F=1-\frac{\sum_{c}n_{c}(n_{c}-1)}{N(N-1)}\quad(2)$$
(unbiased Gini–Simpson, unit-tested vs. brute force); $\pi^{*}=\max_{c}n_{c}/N$. Within groups $G$, weighting pairs equally, $=$ Eq. 2 if $G=\emptyset$:
$$F_{\text{within}}(G)=1-\frac{\sum_{g}\sum_{c}n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}-1)}{\sum_{g}n_{g}(n_{g}-1)}\quad(3)$$
Filable at $\alpha$ iff $\pi^{*}\geq 1-\alpha$. Ceiling $F\leq 1-1/k$: 0.8889 for nine classes; 0.7316 is 82.3% of it.

## 8 The filability protocol

1. Declare space $\mathcal{S}$: defensible axes/levels, each cited.
2. Declare $\varphi$ as deterministic published code, not an LLM.
3. Compute $\pi^{*}$ and $F$ (Eq. 2).
4. Filable at $\alpha$ if $\pi^{*}\geq 1-\alpha$.
5. Report $\pi^{*}$, $F$, per-level discard rates, within-group decompositions.

Regulator need not adjudicate correct choices.

## 9 Limitations

- One model, one task; larger models' effect on $F$ unclear. Pre-registered, unrun: 924-cell Pythia-160m replication (3 seeds), criteria committed; reported either way. Second task designed, unrun.
- Size is an outcome; it distorted $F$, null direction, and functional-gap sign. Fixing it drops $F$ 0.7316→0.2746, more than any axis.
- Space is as wide as the library: optimal ablation absent, so $F$ is a lower bound.
- Discard 52.3%, metric-imbalanced; stated, not adjusted.
- Bootstrap invalid where groups hold 2–5 specs (self-pairs dominate): point estimates with diagnostics; no post-hoc bias-corrected estimator.

## 10 Discussion

No single knob: metric removes 0.1377 of 0.7316. A broken exported objective reflects tooling maturity, not criticism of its authors. Evidentiary weight is measurable, cheaply relative to the sweep.

## 11 Reproducibility

Pre-registration tag prereg-p1-confirmatory. Numbers trace to config, seed, environment fingerprint; single environment across 1,320 cells; code commit recovered via archive vs. git (22/22 files identical). Analysis needs no GPU. Verification: 36 checks, 0 failures, $F$ via three routes incl. brute force; manuscript numbers machine-checked; tables emitted from results; 343 tests.

# Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability

The EU AI Act requires high-risk providers to file technical documentation on how the system decides. We test whether circuit-discovery evidence survives two competent analysts using the same system and tool with different defensible settings. A pre-registered crossed grid of seven analytic axes (every level from a published implementation) feeds a deterministic map from circuits to Annex IV statements. Over 15,840 specifications on GPT-2 small/IOI (7,561 yield a claim), the statement flips on 73.2% of pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738) and the modal claim holds 41.1%. Standardising the metric leaves 59.4%; removing size from the claim and fixing it leaves 27.1% (CI 0.255–0.286). Median pairwise Jaccard is 4% and κ=0.015.

## 1 Introduction

An audit means two auditors reach the same conclusion. Reg. (EU) 2024/1689 (consolidated, amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, CELEX 02024R1689-20260727, read 11 Aug 2026):
- Annex IV 2(b): "the general logic of the AI system and of the algorithms";
- 2(e): "an assessment of the technical measures needed to facilitate the interpretation of the outputs";
- Art. 86(1): "clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken".

We propose no new method and do not call interpretability worthless.

Contributions:
- (i) pre-registered seven-axis multiverse plus a deterministic circuit→Annex IV map;
- (ii) filability criterion π*≥1−α, measured;
- (iii) instability survives standardising any axis, removing size from the claim, and fixing size;
- (iv) when specifications select objects of different sizes, pooled statistics can invert; three of ours do.

## 2 Related work

- **Non-identifiability.** A unique explanation need not exist. We measure its cost when an explanation is filed.
- **Faithfulness metric sensitivity.** Ablation-based faithfulness is highly sensitive to minor choices, so scores reflect researcher choices. That is one axis; we cross seven. Their library is our instrument, so this is a stress test by its own definitions.
- **Structure versus function.** Structurally distinct circuits can implement the same computation ("phantom specialisation"). If so, flip rate would measure which equivalence-class member was sampled. §7.6 answers this functionally: our circuits are not interchangeable.
- **Variance as estimation.** MI as statistical estimation; seed variance is one of our axes.
- **Auditability.** Prior calls for auditing standards to certify findings, and for standardised evaluation across methods. We supply a measurement and criterion; certification needs standardised specification.
- **Multiverse method.** We use the multiverse and the specification curve; undisclosed analytic flexibility can manufacture stability claims.
- **Explanation metrics under optimisation pressure.** Sufficiency and comprehensiveness can be inflated without changing predictions. Both are among our four metrics, so we report per-metric discard rates.

## 3 What this paper is not claiming

- That circuits are no better than random: at fixed size they beat a size-matched null, 0.2746 vs 0.4230.
- That mechanisms agree: functional instability is 0.3972 pooled, 0.4777 at smallest circuits.
- That one mechanism is redescribed: κ=0.0146.
- That seeds matter: the seed selects prompts (evaluation-set variability).
- Anything about scale.

## 4 Formalism

Specification s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g) has components: objective, ablation, corruption distribution, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, granularity. No level was invented. C(s)⊆E with |E|=32491 for GPT-2 small (factorised q/k/v). This is confirmed from the instrument and in closed form:
- block-b attention takes 1+13b sources × 3 slots × 12 heads;
- MLP b takes those sources plus own-block heads;
- the output takes all 157 non-terminal sources.

Circuits draw on 156 components (144 heads, 12 MLPs).

D(s_i,s_j)=1−|C_i∩C_j|/|C_i∪C_j| (1); J̄ = mean Jaccard over unordered pairs.

With φ: circuit→Annex IV statement, F=1−Σ_c n_c(n_c−1)/(N(N−1)) (2). This is unbiased Gini–Simpson, unit-tested against brute force. π*=max_c n_c/N.

F_within(G)=1−Σ_gΣ_c n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}−1)/Σ_g n_g(n_g−1) (3). It weights pairs equally and equals (2) for empty G.

Filable at α iff π*≥1−α. F≤1−1/k; with 9 classes the ceiling is 0.8889, and 0.7316 is 82.3% of it.

# Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability

Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation. Ajay Pravin Mahale, 12 August 2026.

**Abstract.** Does circuit-discovery evidence for EU AI Act technical documentation survive two competent analysts using the same system and tool with different defensible settings? We use a pre-registered crossed grid of seven analytic axes, every level from a published implementation, with circuits mapped deterministically to structured Annex IV statements. On GPT-2 small/IOI we ran 15,840 specifications, of which 7,561 produced a claim. The statement flips on 73.2% of pairs, the modal claim holds 41.1%, and filability fails at every plausible tolerance. Circuits are near-disjoint (median Jaccard 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (κ=0.015). One of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library's canonical task.

## 1 Introduction

Reg. (EU) 2024/1689, as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744 (CELEX 02024R1689-20260727, read 11 Aug 2026), requires:
- Annex IV 2(b): "the general logic of the AI system and of the algorithms";
- 2(e): "an assessment of the technical measures needed to facilitate the interpretation of the outputs";
- Art. 86(1): "clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken".

A filed circuit account has value only if a second analyst with the same system and tool would file something compatible. We propose no new discovery method and do not call interpretability worthless.

Contributions:
- (i) A pre-registered 7-axis multiverse plus a deterministic circuit→Annex IV map.
- (ii) A filability criterion π\*≥1−α, with its measured value.
- (iii) Instability survives standardising any axis, removing size from the claim, and holding size fixed.
- (iv) Where specifications select objects of different sizes, pooled statistics can invert; three of ours do.

## 4 Formalism

- block-b attention: 1+13b sources × 3 slots × 12 heads;
- MLP b: those sources plus own heads;
- output: all 157 non-terminal sources.

There are 156 components (144 heads, 12 MLPs).

D(s_i,s_j)=1−|C_i∩C_j|/|C_i∪C_j| (1); J̄ is the mean pairwise Jaccard.

φ maps a circuit to an Annex IV statement.

## 8 The filability protocol

1. Declare space S: defensible axes and levels, each cited.
2. Declare φ as deterministic published code, not an LLM.
3. Compute π\* and F (Eq. 2) over S.
4. Filable at α if π\*≥1−α.
5. Report π\*, F, per-level discard rates, and within-group decompositions of pooled statistics.

The regulator need not adjudicate which choice is correct.

# Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability

The EU AI Act requires high-risk providers to file technical documentation on how the system decides. We test whether circuit-discovery evidence survives two competent analysts using the same system and tool with different defensible settings. A pre-registered crossed grid of seven analytic axes (every level from a published implementation) feeds a deterministic map from circuits to Annex IV statements. Over 15,840 specifications on GPT-2 small/IOI (7,561 yield a claim), the statement flips on 73.2% of pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738) and the modal claim holds 41.1%. Standardising the metric leaves 59.4%; removing size from the claim and fixing it leaves 27.1% (CI 0.255–0.286). Median pairwise Jaccard is 4% and κ=0.015.

## 8 The filability protocol

1. Declare space 𝒮: axes and defensible levels, each cited.
2. Declare φ as deterministic published code, not an LM.
3. Compute π* and F (Eq. 2).
4. Filable at α if π*≥1−α.
5. Report π*, F, per-level discard rates, within-group decompositions.

The regulator need not judge which choice is correct.

## 9 Limitations

- **One model, one task.** Larger models give band and size more room; the direction of the effect on F is unclear. Pre-registered, unrun: a 924-cell Pythia-160m replication, identical except 3 seeds, with replication criteria timestamped; reported either way. A second task is designed, not run.
- **Circuit size is an outcome, not an axis.** It distorted pooled F, null direction and functional-gap sign. Fixing it drops F 0.7316→0.2746, more than any axis.
- **The multiverse is as wide as the library, not the literature.** Optimal ablation is unimplemented, so F is a lower bound.
- **The discard rate is high and uneven.** 52.3%, metric-imbalanced, stated rather than adjusted.
- **The bootstrap is invalid for one reported family.** With 2–5-specification groups, self-pairs dominate; point estimates only. No post hoc estimator was built.

## 10 Discussion

#### What standardising one axis buys.

No single knob fixes it: the metric removes only 0.1377 of 0.7316.

#### On the instrument.

One of seven exported objectives fails on the library's canonical task. This is a tooling-maturity observation, not the headline.

#### What a regulator can take from this.

Evidentiary weight is measurable, cheaply relative to the sweep.

## 11 Reproducibility

Pre-registration tag: prereg-p1-confirmatory, committed before the sweep. Every number traces to config, seed and environment fingerprint. A single environment across 1,320 cells was verified from the archive; the code commit was recovered by content-addressing (22/22 files). Analysis runs without a GPU. Verification: 36 checks, 0 failures; F by three routes incl. brute force. Every manuscript number and table derives from stored results. 343 tests.

- **The multiverse is as wide as the library, not the literature.** Optimal ablation is unimplemented, so F is a lower bound.
- **The discard rate is high and uneven.** 52.3%, metric-imbalanced, stated rather than adjusted.
- **The bootstrap is invalid for one reported family.** With 2–5-specification groups, self-pairs dominate; point estimates only. No post hoc estimator was built.

## 10 Discussion

#### What standardising one axis buys.

No single knob fixes it: the metric removes only 0.1377 of 0.7316.

#### On the instrument.

One of seven exported objectives fails on the library's canonical task. This is a tooling-maturity observation, not the headline.

#### What a regulator can take from this.

Evidentiary weight is measurable, cheaply relative to the sweep.

{"id": "q128", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the null's flip rate already as low as 0.1421 at 500 edges, although it collapses to one class only at 1,000 edges?", "answer": "GPT-2 small has only 156 components among 32,491 edges. {"id": "q130", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why must at least about four fifths of the 28,580,580 specification pairs have a pairwise D of 0.5 or more, whatever edges the circuits contain?", "answer": "Circuits come in ten sizes, and neighbouring sizes differ by a factor of at least 2. ZK7 is given as a standalone protocol, one of the seven documented discovery objectives does not execute at all on the library’s own canonical task, and the study covering one model and one task leaves untested whether the conclusion holds at scale. The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to file technical documentation describing how the system reaches its decisions, mechanistic interpretability being the obvious source of such evidence and circuit discovery its most developed instrument, and whether that evidence survives the condition under which it would be relied upon, namely 2 competent analysts, the same system, the same tool, different defensible settings, is what is asked, a crossed grid of seven analytic axes having been pre-registered, every level taken from a published implementation, with each discovered circuit mapped through a deterministic QM3 to a structured Annex IV statement.

A filing that cannot state its own $\pi^{*}$ has not been audited but has merely been asserted, and the satisfaction of ZK7 at tolerance $\alpha$ by a filed interpretability claim $c$ derived from a circuit is constituted by the inequality $\pi^{*}\geq 1-\alpha$ (obligation 4), the quantity $\pi^{*}=\max_{c}n_{c}/N$ being computed over the specification space $\mathcal{S}$ and $F$ being obtained by Equation 2 (obligation 3), with $\pi^{*}$, $F$, the EX9 per axis level and the within-group decomposition of any pooled statistic all to be reported (obligation 5), these being determinations which presuppose the prior discharge of obligations 1 and 2, namely the declaration of $\mathcal{S}$—the analytic axes and the levels of each that a competent analyst could defend, each with a citation—and the declaration of QM3 $\varphi$ as deterministic, published code and not a language model; no adjudication by the regulator of which analytic choice is correct is required by the protocol, which is the property that makes it implementable, only that the filer declare the space and report how much of it agrees.

ANSWER Q1: Contradicted. The early-versus-late contradiction concerns the overseer claim, whereas the affected-person map leads with input segment rather than layer band.

ANSWER Q2: Yes. With three classes and a modal share of at least 0.80, the largest possible flip rate is about \(1-(0.8^2+0.1^2+0.1^2)=0.34\), well below the observed 0.4543; therefore \(\pi^*<0.80\).

ANSWER Q3: Supported. At affected-person COARSE granularity, the modal input-segment claim has share \(\pi^*=0.7291\), so a majority would give the same explanation, although this still fails the paper’s 0.80 filability criterion.

ANSWER Q4: Yes. At 500 edges, discovered circuits have \(F=0.4258\), versus \(0.1421\) for the size-matched random null.

ANSWER Q5: Yes, assuming the functional results remained unchanged. The rebuttal rests on low κ and differing per-example behavior showing that the circuits are not functionally interchangeable, not on the structural distance statistic alone.

ANSWER Q6: About 4.13 times as large. Applying the formula gives approximately 134,245 edges for 24 blocks, compared with 32,491 for GPT-2 small.

ANSWER Q7: The middle band accounts for only 8.5% of claims. Early and late claims account for 47.9% and 43.6%, respectively, so early-versus-late disagreements alone contribute roughly \(2(0.479)(0.436)\approx0.418\) to the flip rate.

ANSWER Q8: No. The seven reductions sum to 0.2540, which would lower \(F\) only from 0.7316 to about 0.4776, still well above 0.20.

ANSWER Q9: The H4 comparison \(F-(1-\text{agreement})>0.10\), described as filings differing more than mechanisms, would become uninterpretable. Language-model variance in \(\phi\) would be confounded with filing instability.

ANSWER Q10: No. Equal weighting of the ten rows gives mean discovered \(F\approx0.3858\) and mean null \(F\approx0.3563\), so discovered circuits would instead appear slightly less stable.

ANSWER Q11: The limitation is that the multiverse covers the implementation library, not the full literature; for example, optimal ablation was unimplemented. Thus a filed \(\pi^*\) is conditional on the declared space and may overstate agreement across all defensible choices.

ANSWER Q12: Removing the size label from \(\phi\) does not remove size variation among the selected circuits, which can still change their dominant layer band. Holding circuit size fixed removes that major source of variation, reducing \(F\) much further.

ANSWER Q13: Supported. Affected-person \(F\) is lower than overseer \(F\) at COARSE (0.3950 vs 0.5733), MEDIUM (0.6597 vs 0.7316), and FINE (0.6744 vs 0.7681).

ANSWER Q14: The statement that “at both ends, mechanisms differ more than filings” would lose support at the smallest-size end. A functional instability of 0.30 would be below the 10-edge filing flip rate of 0.4543.

ANSWER Q15: The Section 7.4 fixed-size, layer-only result would be most vulnerable. Its \(F=0.2706\) is much closer to 0.20 than the main H2 result of 0.7316, making a post hoc 0.20 cutoff look tailored to preserve a positive finding.

ANSWER Q16: The interpretation that the 73% filing flip reflects genuinely different, noninterchangeable mechanisms would lose its main defence. High κ would instead suggest that circuits agree on examples beyond chance and may be redescriptions of substantially the same mechanism.

ANSWER Q17: Not settled. The 47.9% early-layer share describes the dominant-band claims produced across analytic specifications, not where GPT-2 small primarily performs the IOI computation, and it is not even a majority.

ANSWER Q18: The claim that the failure set was exactly one complete discovery-objective arm would lose support. Scattered failures would make exclusion by a single objective less clearly justified.

ANSWER Q19: For one objective there are 22 valid ablation/corruption combinations—two ablations that ignore corruption plus five ablations crossed with four corruptions—times two prompts and five seeds. Thus \(22\times2\times5=220\) cells.

ANSWER Q20: No. With four classes and \(\pi^*=0.80\), distributing the remaining 0.20 equally permits a flip rate of about \(1-(0.8^2+3(0.2/3)^2)=0.3467\), so the observed 0.3380 is compatible with filability.

ANSWER Q1: Contradicted. Early-versus-late layer bands are overseer attributions; the affected-person claims concern input segments, so the paper does not show affected persons receiving contradictory layer explanations.

ANSWER Q2: Yes. The 10-edge discovered flip rate of 0.4777 is too high to be compatible with any claim receiving at least 80% support, even allowing for the reported number of classes, so it implies failure at α = 0.20 within that restricted space.

ANSWER Q3: Not settled. The finite declared specification space is not established as a representative distribution over analysts, and a pairwise flip rate alone does not justify the population claim that most analysts would select the same coarsest input-segment explanation.

ANSWER Q4: Yes. Table 7’s 500-edge row has a higher flip rate for discovered circuits than for the size-matched random null, despite the aggregate within-size comparison favoring discovered circuits.

ANSWER Q5: No. A median pairwise D near 0.2 would indicate substantial structural overlap, leaving phantom specialisation—or many nominally different circuits encoding nearly the same structure—as a plausible explanation.

ANSWER Q6: About 4.1 times larger. Under the paper’s scheme, doubling the number of blocks while keeping 12 heads makes the dominant cross-layer edge term grow approximately quadratically: roughly 134,000 edges rather than GPT-2 small’s 32,500.

ANSWER Q7: Because middle-layer claims are too rare to generate a 0.5733 pairwise flip rate by themselves. Much of the disagreement must therefore consist of direct early-versus-late assignments, not merely pairs involving the middle band.

ANSWER Q8: Yes. Under the hypothetical additive assumption, the seven Table 6 reductions would take the projected flip rate below 0.20, although the paper does not assume that reductions actually combine additively.

ANSWER Q9: The preregistered discovered-circuit versus size-matched-random-null comparison would become uninterpretable. Its claim-level difference could then reflect stochastic or model-dependent behavior in φ rather than differences between the two circuit populations.

ANSWER Q10: Yes. Equal-weighting the ten size rows still leaves the discovered-circuit average below the random-null average, so the reported direction is not solely an artifact of Equation 3’s pair weighting.

ANSWER Q11: The study acknowledges that its declared space covers only enumerated implementation and analysis choices, not every defensible choice an analyst might make. Thus a filed π* is auditable and fixed relative to that space, but is not guaranteed to remain stable or uniquely justified in a broader space.

ANSWER Q12: Removing the size field changes only the claim encoding, while circuits of different sizes can still differ on all the remaining claim components. Holding size fixed also removes the substantial cross-size compositional variation, hence the much larger reduction from 0.5733 to 0.2706.

ANSWER Q13: Supported. Table 4 reports lower affected-person flip rates than overseer flip rates at each matched coarse, medium, and fine granularity, although that comparison is confined to the declared space and GPT-2 small IOI.

ANSWER Q14: The claim that discovered circuits are less stable than the size-matched null at the smallest end would lose support. Lowering the smallest-circuit rate from 0.4777 to about 0.30 would remove the reported small-size exception to the overall stability advantage.

ANSWER Q15: The overseer-medium H2/Section 7.4 filability result would be most vulnerable. If 0.20 were chosen after seeing the sweep, the declaration that the observed instability crosses the permitted threshold could reasonably be viewed as threshold fitting.

ANSWER Q16: The interpretation that the 73% flip rate reflects severe substantive disagreement rather than a prevalence or label-distribution artifact would lose its main defence. High kappa would indicate strong chance-corrected agreement despite the raw flip statistic.

ANSWER Q17: Not settled. The paper studies how circuit-discovery and reporting choices alter layer-attribution claims; it does not establish that GPT-2 small’s underlying IOI computation occurs mainly in early layers.

ANSWER Q18: The statement that the exclusion was confined to one non-executing discovery objective would lose support. Scattered failures would instead suggest that exclusions affected multiple objectives and potentially the comparative results.

ANSWER Q19: That objective occupies one complete slice of the factorial sweep. Crossing its single objective level with all 220 combinations of the remaining axes yields exactly 220 non-executing cells.

ANSWER Q20: No. The 20-edge flip rate and class count are still compatible with a sufficiently dominant claim class, so those summary statistics alone do not establish that every possible filed claim has more than 20% disagreement.

ANSWER Q21: The deterministic-coarsening or monotonicity cross-check would be unavailable. Nesting lets the authors verify that a coarse disagreement remains a disagreement at finer levels—and hence that flip rates behave consistently across granularities.

ANSWER Q1: No, not by itself. If all circuits formed a single nested chain, the high D could be generated by cardinality differences while every specification recovered progressively larger portions of the same mechanism.

ANSWER Q2: Only for attainable sizes, and it would become weak near the model’s total edge count. With a few hundred edges, large requested circuits would be impossible or nearly the whole graph, making the size-matched null highly constrained and largely uninformative.

ANSWER Q3: Results depending on the eligible-edge universe—especially random-circuit sampling, null expectations, and any normalization using the total edge count—would be in doubt. Flip rates and claim summaries computed directly from the successfully discovered circuits would not automatically be invalid, although the disagreement would weaken confidence in the implementation generally.

ANSWER Q4: It would threaten the paper’s disclaimer that the instability is not merely a seed or stochastic-search artifact. It would not, by itself, undermine the separate statement that the paper is not establishing which specification is substantively correct.

ANSWER Q5: Corruption does not have a stable effect across ablation operators: some operators react strongly to it, while two do not read it at all. REML therefore attributes the resulting size changes to the operator-specific ablation–corruption interaction rather than to a common corruption main effect.

ANSWER Q6: It could not responsibly say that the excess or deficit of instability was not simply due to circuit-size composition. That statement requires size matching or within-size comparisons, since a pooled random null confounds topology with the distribution of edge counts.

ANSWER Q7: No. At 50 edges, the discovered circuits are more claim-stable than size-matched random edge sets, consistent with the aggregate within-size comparison in which the random null flips more often.

ANSWER Q8: No. If all 220 outputs were still excluded by the precommitted threshold rule, the retained specification set—and hence the numerator and denominator of the reported 0.7316 rate—would be unchanged.

ANSWER Q9: No, not substantively. A degenerate declared space in which every specification returns the same 10,000-edge class could pass the filability test through unanimity even though the filing conveys no discriminating evidence.

ANSWER Q10: The body would need to tolerate approximately α = 0.2706, equivalently requiring no more confidence than the reported modal share of about 0.7294. In general, filability requires α to be at least the nonmodal mass, 1 − π*.

ANSWER Q11: It would inherit the overseer’s layer-band COARSE result: a flip rate of about 0.2706 and a modal share of about 0.7294. Changing the stakeholder label does not change the claim map when both are keyed to the same feature.

ANSWER Q12: They must all yield the MEDIUM class combining the dominant late-layer band with the largest, 10,000-edge size class. The size is fixed and Table 7 indicates a common dominant band for those specifications.

ANSWER Q13: No. COARSE does not encode the size-bin label, so replacing the committed size bins with deciles cannot alter its within-size claim assignments.

ANSWER Q14: The two quantities measure different things. REML’s 78.8% concerns variance in continuous circuit size and includes operator-dependent corruption effects, whereas the 0.0302 reduction concerns crossings of categorical claim boundaries; large size changes can leave the filed claim unchanged.

ANSWER Q15: Yes, potentially, and it would have to be recomputed. MEDIUM includes the size class, so replacing the committed boundaries with deciles changes which pooled specifications share a claim even when the underlying circuits remain unchanged.

ANSWER Q16: Contradicted. Nonzero within-size instability, including at sizes such as 50 edges, shows that claim changes occur beyond the 10-edge circuits; the reported instability is not confined to the smallest threshold.

ANSWER Q17: No. Treating duplicate specifications as independent elements would overweight mechanisms generated by irrelevant crossings, thereby distorting both the modal probability π* and the filability statistic F unless the protocol deduplicated or appropriately reweighted them.

ANSWER Q18: No. Those 2,067 specifications all receive the same 10,000-edge MEDIUM filing class, while their selected edge sets can still differ structurally, so filings do not differ more than mechanisms within that subset.

ANSWER Q19: Not settled. The study demonstrates instability within the examined library and specification multiverse, but without comparable experiments across independent discovery libraries it cannot identify the library itself as the cause.

ANSWER Q20: Adding size class refines categories that the null’s COARSE map had pooled together, and random circuits frequently fall into different such subclasses even when sampling is edge-count matched. The discovered circuits’ size and coarse structural labels are much more aligned, so the refinement creates relatively few additional disagreements there.

ANSWER Q1: No. If every smaller circuit were nested inside every larger one, a high Jaccard distance could result solely from size differences and would not by itself establish distinct mechanisms.

ANSWER Q2: Not necessarily. With only a few hundred possible edges, size-matched random circuits could occupy much of the edge universe and quickly saturate its components, making the null degenerate rather than an informative comparison.

ANSWER Q3: The random-baseline results, chance-overlap calculations, and claims relying on a complete 32,491-edge universe would be in doubt. The directly computed Jaccard distances, claim flip rates, modal shares, and κ from the discovered circuits would not depend on the closed-form universe count, although their interpretation as circuits over the intended GPT-2 graph would merit checking.

ANSWER Q4: It would threaten the statement that the paper is not claiming seeds matter. A large reduction from standardising seed would show that evaluation-set variability induced by seed materially drives claim instability, even if the seed still only selects prompts.

ANSWER Q5: Corruption is nested within and only read by certain ablation operators, so its effect is conditional on the ablation choice rather than an independent additive main effect. REML therefore assigns the variation generated by particular ablation–corruption combinations to their interaction.

ANSWER Q6: It could not have claimed that discovered circuits beat a size-matched random null at fixed size. The pooled comparison points in the opposite direction—0.7316 versus 0.6774—and is reversed only after controlling for size.

ANSWER Q7: No. At 50 edges, discovered circuits have F=0.4639, compared with 0.7310 for the size-matched random null.

ANSWER Q8: No. If every added specification were discarded, the retained set used to compute F would be unchanged, so the headline value would remain 0.7316.

ANSWER Q9: No. The criterion would label that space perfectly filable because all 10,000-edge circuits yield one claim, but it does not test whether that stability comes from informative evidence or from saturation and lack of variation.

ANSWER Q10: It would need to accept α≥0.5212, or at least 52.12% non-modal claims. The modal share is 0.4788, and filability requires π*≥1−α.

ANSWER Q11: It would have F=0.5733 and a modal share of 0.4788. Keying it on dominant layer band would reproduce the overseer COARSE three-band distribution.

ANSWER Q12: They must all yield the “early, distributed” class. A 10,000-edge circuit is distributed, and early-distributed is the only distributed class in Table 4 with enough observations to contain all 2,067 specifications.

ANSWER Q13: No. Section 7.4 removes size from the claim and compares circuits at fixed edge size, so changing the size-bin boundaries would not affect its layer-band-only F=0.2706.

ANSWER Q14: The REML result concerns variance in continuous log circuit size, whereas the flip rate concerns categorical filing claims. Moreover, much of the size variance is produced by specific ablation–corruption combinations, so fixing ablation alone leaves corruption and the other claim-generating variation in place.

ANSWER Q15: Yes. Table 1 reports F=0.7719 with decile size bins, rather than 0.7316 with the committed bins.

ANSWER Q16: Contradicted. Table 7 shows nonzero discovered-circuit flip rates at every listed size from 10 through 2,000 edges; only the 5,000- and 10,000-edge groups have F=0.

ANSWER Q17: Not generally. Duplicate specifications would receive extra weight in π* and in the pair counts underlying F, potentially making the result reflect accidental duplication rather than the declared analytic choices.

ANSWER Q18: No. The filing flip rate is zero at 10,000 edges, while functional agreement is less than perfect and κ remains low; the paper explicitly says that at the size-range ends mechanisms differ more than filings.

ANSWER Q19: Not settled. The paper stress-tests one library using its own published options and notes a tooling failure, but it does not compare libraries or show that the instability is uniquely caused by this implementation.

# Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability

Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation

Ajay Pravin Mahale

12 August 2026

###### Abstract

The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to file technical
documentation describing how the system reaches its decisions. Circuit discovery
is the most developed instrument of mechanistic interpretability. We test circuit
evidence against cross-analyst variation under fixed system and tooling.

We pre-registered a crossed grid of seven analytic axes, every level taken from a
published implementation, with a deterministic claim map from circuits to
structured Annex IV statements. Across 15,840 pre-registered specifications on
GPT-2 small and indirect object identification, of which 7,561 produced a claim,
the flip rate is 73.2% (95% CI 0.725 to 0.738) and the modal claim commands 41.1%
of the space; the evidence fails filability at every plausible conformity
tolerance.

Standardising the evaluation metric leaves the flip rate at 59.4%. A size-free
claim with size held fixed leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255 to 0.286), above the
pre-registered threshold. Median pairwise Jaccard overlap is 4% and Cohen’s
kappa is 0.015.

We give the filability criterion as a standalone protocol, and report that one of
the seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s own
canonical task. The study covers one model and one task; behaviour at scale is
untested.

## 1 Introduction

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to file
technical documentation. Annex IV point 2(b) asks for “the general logic of the
AI system and of the algorithms”. Point 2(e) asks for “an assessment of the
technical measures needed to facilitate the interpretation of the outputs”.
Article 86(1) gives a person subject to certain automated decisions the right to
“clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the
decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken”. Quotations
are from the consolidated text as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744,
CELEX 02024R1689-20260727, read 11 August 2026.

Circuit discovery, which returns a subgraph attributed to a behaviour, is the
component of mechanistic interpretability with mature tooling and the natural
source of the technical content these provisions request. We quantify the
dispersion of a derived regulatory claim over the space of defensible analytic
specifications and attach a decision rule usable by a standards body. We neither
propose a discovery method nor dispute the value of interpretability; the target
is the evidentiary standard that filing presumes.

#### Contributions.

(i) A pre-registered multiverse over seven analytic axes of circuit discovery,
with every level drawn from a published implementation, and a deterministic map
from circuits to Annex IV statements.
(ii) A filability criterion, $\pi^{*}\geq 1-\alpha$ , applicable in a conformity
procedure, with its measured value on a canonical task.
(iii) Persistence of instability under single-axis standardisation, removal of
circuit size from the claim, and conditioning on size.
(iv) Three pooled statistics in our design that invert under size conditioning,
a hazard for any multiverse whose specifications select objects of different
sizes.

## 2 Related work

#### Non-identifiability.

Méloux et al. [6] show that, under mechanistic interpretability’s own criteria, a
unique explanation for a given behaviour need not exist. We take this as premise
and measure its cost when an explanation is filed rather than published.

#### Faithfulness metric sensitivity.

Miller et al. [8] survey design choices in ablation-based faithfulness measurement,
find existing methods highly sensitive to seemingly insignificant changes, and
conclude that faithfulness scores reflect methodological choices as well as the
circuit. They establish one axis; we cross seven and propagate to a regulatory
statement. Their released library is our instrument, so the study stress-tests
the tooling by its own definitions.

#### Structure versus function.

Bayat Makou et al. [1] vary input statistics at fixed task and find structurally
distinct circuits implementing the same computation, termed phantom
specialisation. Under that hypothesis, a claim flip rate would index sampling
within an equivalence class of behaviourally identical subgraphs. Section 7.6
measures this directly.

#### Variance as estimation.

Méloux et al. [7] treat mechanistic interpretability as statistical estimation
and analyse estimator variance. Seed variance is one axis of our space; their
framing is the statistical companion at the level of the whole specification.

#### Auditability.

Lan et al. [4] document two papers reaching conflicting conclusions about the
same behaviour, with a third finding both partly correct and incomparable, and
call for auditing standards permitting certification in safety-critical settings.
We supply a measurement and a criterion. Sharkey et al. [10] list open problems
including the socio-technical ones touched here, and Mueller et al. [9] argue that
cross-method comparison requires standardised evaluation, adjacent to our
position that certification requires standardised specification.

#### Multiverse method.

The design follows Steegen et al. [13] on reporting across defensible
data-processing choices and Simonsohn et al. [12], whose specification curve we
adapt. Simmons et al. [11] identified undisclosed analytic flexibility as the
mechanism by which almost anything can be presented as significant; a stability
claim about an explanation is susceptible to the same mechanism.

#### Explanation metrics under optimisation pressure.

Hsia et al. [3] show that sufficiency and comprehensiveness can be inflated
without changing predictions or explanations. Both are among our four evaluation
metrics, and discard rates are reported per metric.

## 3 What this paper is not claiming

Two of the following were positions we held before the decompositions were run.

At fixed circuit size, discovered circuits are more stable than a size-matched
random null, 0.2746 against 0.4230.

Functional instability is 0.3972 pooled and 0.4777 at the smallest circuits.

Cohen’s kappa is 0.0146.

The seed selects which prompts are sampled; it encodes evaluation-set
variability, not nondeterminism.

One model, one task; no claim about scale.

## 4 Formalism

A specification is a tuple $s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)$ , with $o$ the discovery
objective, $a$ the ablation operator, $d$ the corruption distribution, $m$ the
evaluation metric, $\tau$ the size threshold, $P$ the prompt variant, $r$ the seed
and $g$ the granularity. Every level of every axis is taken from a published
implementation.

Discovery returns $C(s)\subseteq E$ . For GPT-2 small under the factorised graph
with separate query, key and value inputs, $|E|=32{,}491$ , confirmed from the
instrument and from a closed-form count over the computation order: block $b$
attention receives from $1+13b$ sources at three input slots for each of 12 heads,
MLP $b$ receives from those sources plus its own block’s heads, and the output
receives from all 157 non-terminal sources. Components are drawn from 144
attention heads and 12 MLPs, 156 in total.

#### Circuit instability.

| | $D(s_{i},s_{j})=1-\frac{|C_{i}\cap C_{j}|}{|C_{i}\cup C_{j}|},$

## 6 Method

#### Model and task.

GPT-2 small on indirect object identification [15], the scale of the
non-identifiability and faithfulness literature extended here; the edge count
supports a size-matched random baseline.

#### Grid.

Seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four corruption
distributions nested within the five operators that read them, four metrics,
three thresholds, two prompt variants, five seeds: 1,540 discovery cells and
18,480 specifications as pre-registered. Corruption is nested because two
ablation operators never read the corrupt distribution, and crossing would emit
duplicate specifications. Discovery uses the edge attribution patching family
[14] and integrated edge gradients as implemented in the library released with
Miller et al. [8]; the automated circuit discovery lineage is Conmy et al. [2].
Corruption levels follow Wang et al. [15].

#### Pre-registration.

The analysis plan was committed and tagged before the confirmatory sweep, with
both abstracts drafted in advance. Deviations are recorded in an append-only file
with dates and whether each was decided before or after the affected result was
seen.

#### Statistics.

No $p$ -value is computed across specifications [13, 12]. Uncertainty is from a
nonparametric bootstrap resampling specifications, never pairs, at $B=10{,}000$ ,

the grid.

All 220 cells of one discovery objective raise a runtime error from a mean
squared error computed against an integral target inside the library’s own code.
A digest over the sorted failing cell identifiers confirms the failure set is

realised grid is six objectives, 1,320 cells and 15,840 specifications.

## 8 The filability protocol

Filability of an interpretability claim. For a filed claim $c$
derived from a circuit:

1.

Declare the specification space $\mathcal{S}$ : the analytic axes and the
levels of each that a competent analyst could defend, each with a citation.

2.

Declare the claim map $\varphi$ as deterministic, published code. Not a
language model.

3.

Compute $\pi^{*}=\max_{c}n_{c}/N$ over $\mathcal{S}$ , and $F$ by
Equation 2.

4.

The claim is filable at tolerance $\alpha$ if $\pi^{*}\geq 1-\alpha$ .

5.

Report $\pi^{*}$ , $F$ , the discard rate per axis level, and the
within-group decomposition of any pooled statistic.

The protocol requires declaration of the space and the agreeing fraction, not
adjudication of the correct analytic choice.

## 9 Limitations

#### One model, one task.

Larger models widen both layer band and size class, with no obvious sign of the
effect on $F$ . A second-model replication is pre-registered but not yet run: a
924-cell grid on Pythia-160m, a different architecture family performing the
same task, identical on every axis except three seed levels rather than five. The
analysis plan, reduced grid, and replication/refutation criteria are committed
and timestamped before any cell ran, and will be reported in a revision in either
direction. A second task is designed and not run.

#### Circuit size is an outcome, not an axis.

Size is set by the threshold rule and distorts three pooled quantities: $F$ , the
direction of the null comparison, and the sign of the functional gap.
Conditioning on it drops $F$ from 0.7316 to 0.2746, more than standardising any
pre-registered axis. Every pooled statistic is reported with its within-size
decomposition.

#### The multiverse is as wide as the library, not the literature.

Optimal ablation [5] is a defensible operator the instrument does not implement;
the measured $F$ is a lower bound relative to the field’s full choice set.

#### The discard rate is high and uneven.

52.3%, with a metric-imbalanced pool. The threshold rule was fixed in advance and
no failing item repaired; composition is stated, not adjusted.

#### The bootstrap is invalid for one reported family.

Where conditioning groups hold two to five specifications, retained self-pairs
dominate and intervals are unusable; those quantities are point estimates with
the diagnostic attached. No bias-corrected estimator was constructed post hoc.

#### Positioning of the evidence.

The grid fixes the system, the instrument, and the task; all variation is over
analytic choices sourced from published implementations. Specifications differ
only in the levels of the seven declared axes, and every circuit enters the claim
map through identical code.

## 10 Discussion

#### What standardising one axis buys.

The metric removes 0.1377 of a 0.7316 flip rate; no single axis suffices.

#### On the instrument.

One of seven documented, publicly exported discovery objectives does not run on
the library’s own canonical task. It is treated as a discard with its rate and as
an observation on the maturity of tooling under regulatory reliance, not as a
criticism of a library whose authors call for exactly this work [10].

#### What a regulator can take from this.

Evidentiary weight is measurable, and the measurement is cheap relative to the
sweep producing the circuit.

## 11 Reproducibility

The pre-registration is a timestamped commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory
in the public repository, made before the confirmatory sweep. Every reported
number traces to a config, a seed and an environment fingerprint. The
confirmatory sweep ran under a single environment across all 1,320 cells,
verified from the results archive, and the code commit was recovered by
content-addressed comparison of the uploaded archive against the git tree,
22 of 22 files identical. The analysis layer runs without a GPU.

A verification script recomputes every headline quantity from raw results and
asserts against reported values: 36 checks, 0 failures, with $F$ derived by
three routes including brute-force pairwise computation. A second script checks
every numeric token in the manuscript against values derived from stored
results. Tables are emitted directly from results. The test suite is 343 tests.
