# Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability

Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation

Ajay Pravin Mahale

12 August 2026

###### Abstract

The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to file technical
documentation describing how the system reaches its decisions. Mechanistic
interpretability is the obvious source of such evidence, and circuit discovery is
its most developed instrument. We ask what it would take for that evidence to
serve the purpose for which it would be filed: to be read, checked and relied upon
by parties other than the analyst who produced it.

We set out a pre-registered crossed grid of seven analytic axes for circuit
discovery on GPT-2 small and the indirect object identification task, with every
level taken from a published implementation. We describe how each axis enters the
discovery pipeline, why each level is defensible, and how the choices interact
with the size of the circuit that is ultimately selected. Alongside the grid we
describe a deterministic summary of discovered circuits in the vocabulary of
Annex IV, intended to make circuit-level output legible to documentation readers
without introducing the variance of a generative model.

The paper is primarily a framework and a design. We argue that circuit-level
evidence should be accompanied by an explicit declaration of the analytic choices
behind it, that those choices are numerous and individually well motivated, and
that documentation practice has not yet caught up with this fact. We close with a
set of reporting recommendations and an account of the limitations of a study
built on one model and one task.

## 1 Introduction

An audit means two auditors reach the same conclusion. That is not a definition
borrowed from machine learning; it is what makes an audit worth commissioning.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to file
technical documentation. Annex IV point 2(b) asks for “the general logic of the
AI system and of the algorithms”. Point 2(e) asks for “an assessment of the
technical measures needed to facilitate the interpretation of the outputs”.
Article 86(1) gives a person subject to certain automated decisions the right to
“clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the
decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken”. These are
quoted from the consolidated text as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744,
CELEX 02024R1689-20260727, read 11 August 2026.

Mechanistic interpretability offers to supply the technical content. Circuit
discovery produces a subgraph said to explain a behaviour, and it is the part of
the field with mature tooling. If a provider files a circuit-level account of why
its system behaved as it did, the filing is worth something only if a second
analyst, given the same system and the same tool, would file something compatible.

That premise is rarely examined. Circuit discovery is not a single procedure but a
family of procedures, each parameterised by choices that the literature treats as
methodological detail: which objective scores an edge, which operator removes it,
what the model is shown in its place, how the result is evaluated, and where the
cut-off is drawn. Each of these choices has a published rationale. Each has been
used in peer-reviewed work. None is wrong. A provider preparing documentation
could pick any of them and defend the pick.

This paper takes that observation seriously as a matter of documentation design.
We do not propose a better circuit discovery method, and we do not argue that
interpretability is worthless. We argue that circuit-level evidence carries with
it a space of analytic choices, that this space should be declared rather than
left implicit, and that a documentation regime which ignores it is assuming
something it has not checked.

#### Contributions.

(i) A pre-registered multiverse over seven analytic axes of circuit discovery,
with every level drawn from a published implementation.
(ii) A deterministic, published map from circuits to structured Annex IV
statements, designed so that summarising a circuit adds no variance of its own.
(iii) An analysis of how circuit size arises as a consequence of the threshold
rule rather than as a design choice, and why this matters for any study that
compares objects selected under different specifications.
(iv) A set of reporting recommendations that a standards body or conformity
assessment body could adopt without having to adjudicate which analytic choice is
correct.

## 2 Related work

#### Non-identifiability.

Méloux et al. [6] ask whether, for a given
behaviour and under mechanistic interpretability’s own criteria, a unique
explanation exists, and answer that it need not. Our premise is theirs. Our
contribution is downstream: we consider what non-identifiability implies when an
explanation is filed rather than published, and what a filer ought to disclose as
a consequence.

#### Faithfulness metric sensitivity.

Miller et al. [8] survey design
choices in ablation-based faithfulness measurement and find existing methods
highly sensitive to seemingly insignificant changes, concluding that faithfulness
scores reflect the researcher’s methodological choices as well as the circuit.
They establish that one axis matters. We extend the design to seven crossed axes
and frame the result in terms of documentation. Their released library is the
instrument we use, which means our design is built on the tooling’s own
definitions rather than on reimplementations that could introduce discrepancies
of their own.

#### Structure versus function.

Bayat Makou et al. [1] vary input
statistics while holding the task fixed and find that structurally distinct
circuits implement the same computation, a pattern they term phantom
specialisation. This is an important consideration for any design of our kind: if
discovery merely samples from an equivalence class of behaviourally identical
subgraphs, then structural differences between circuits need not imply
differences that a documentation reader should care about. We discuss how a
functional measurement can address this in Section 7.6.

#### Variance as estimation.

Méloux et al. [7] treat mechanistic
interpretability as statistical estimation and analyse the variance of the
estimator. Seed variance is one axis of our space; their framing is the natural
statistical companion to what we do at the level of the whole specification, and
it suggests that circuit-level claims should be reported with an account of their
sampling behaviour in the same way that any other estimate would be.

#### Auditability.

Lan et al. [4] observe that two papers reached
conflicting conclusions about the same behaviour, with a third finding both partly
correct and incomparable, and call for auditing standards so that findings can be
certified in safety-critical settings. We answer that call with a design and a
set of reporting conventions. Sharkey et al. [10] list open problems in the
field, including the socio-technical ones this paper touches, and
Mueller et al. [9] argue that comparison across methods requires standardised
evaluation, which is adjacent to our argument that certification requires a
declared specification.

#### Multiverse method.

The design follows Steegen et al. [13], who propose
reporting results across the space of defensible data-processing choices, and
Simonsohn et al. [12], whose specification curve is a natural visualisation for
designs of this kind. Simmons et al. [11] named the underlying problem: undisclosed
flexibility in analysis lets an analyst present almost anything as significant. We
are applying a psychology methods literature to a machine learning evidentiary
question, and the transfer is not decorative. The claim that an explanation is
stable is exactly the kind of claim that flexibility can manufacture, and exactly
the kind of claim that disclosure of the analytic space can discipline.

#### Explanation metrics under optimisation pressure.

Hsia et al. [3] show that sufficiency and comprehensiveness can be inflated
without changing predictions or explanations. Two of our four evaluation metrics
are those two, which is one reason we treat the metric as a first-class axis and
recommend that any discard rule be reported per metric rather than pooled
silently.

## 3 What this paper is not claiming

Stated early because each is a reading the paper does not support.

We are not claiming that discovered circuits are no better than random. The
literature on circuit discovery has repeatedly shown that discovered subgraphs
carry information about the behaviour under study, and nothing in our design is
intended to dispute that.

Nor that any particular discovery objective, ablation operator or metric is
incorrect. Every level in our grid has a published justification, and the point of
including it is that a competent analyst could choose it.

Nor that random seeds are the main concern. The seed here selects which prompts are
sampled, so it is evaluation-set variability rather than nondeterminism, and it is
one axis among seven.

Nor that the regulation is misconceived. The documentation requirements are
reasonable; the question is what technical evidence can meet them and what must
accompany that evidence.

And nothing at all about scale. One model, one task.

## 4 Formalism

A specification is a tuple of analytic choices
$s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)$ , with $o$ the discovery objective, $a$ the
ablation operator, $d$ the corruption distribution, $m$ the evaluation metric,
$\tau$ the size threshold, $P$ the prompt variant, $r$ the seed and $g$ the
granularity. Every level of every axis is taken from a published implementation.
None was invented for this study.

Circuit discovery returns $C(s)\subseteq E$ , a subset of the model’s edge set.
For GPT-2 small under the factorised graph with separate query, key and value
inputs, $|E|=32{,}491$ . We confirm this from the instrument and independently
from a closed-form count over the computation order: block $b$ attention receives
from $1+13b$ sources at three input slots for each of 12 heads, MLP $b$ receives
from those sources plus its own block’s heads, and the output receives from all
157 non-terminal sources. Circuits touch components drawn from 144 attention heads
and 12 MLPs, so 156 in total.

#### Circuit instability.

For two specifications, a natural structural comparison is

| | $D(s_{i},s_{j})=1-\frac{|C_{i}\cap C_{j}|}{|C_{i}\cup C_{j}|},$
| | (1)

and $\bar{J}$ denotes the mean Jaccard similarity over unordered pairs. Jaccard
distance is the standard choice for comparing edge sets and is easy to compute
exactly when the number of distinct circuits is modest. Its main weakness, which
matters later, is that its chance level depends strongly on circuit size: two
large random subsets of $E$ overlap far more than two small ones, so any
comparison of structural overlap must be read against the sizes involved.

#### Claim instability.

Let $\varphi$ map a circuit to a structured
Annex IV statement. Two circuits produce compatible documentation when $\varphi$
assigns them the same statement, and incompatible documentation otherwise. This
binary view is deliberately coarse. It ignores degrees of similarity between
statements, because a documentation reader does not receive a similarity score;
they receive a statement, and either it agrees with the statement a second analyst
would have produced or it does not. The nesting of granularities described in
Section 5 means that the coarseness can be tuned: at a coarse granularity many
circuits share a statement, and at a fine granularity few do.

#### Filability.

Whether circuit-level evidence is suitable for filing
is ultimately a question for the procedure that receives it. What a technical
paper can contribute is a clear statement of the information that procedure would
need: the space of analytic choices the evidence was drawn from, the deterministic
rule by which evidence was turned into a statement, and the extent to which the
statement depends on choices within that space. A filing that omits these leaves
the receiving body unable to tell whether the evidence reflects the system or the
analyst.

## 5 The claim map

$\varphi$ is the most attackable choice in the paper, so it is fixed in the
pre-registration, implemented as deterministic code, and published. It is not
generated by a language model; doing so would introduce model variance on top of
circuit variance with no way to separate them, and would make the statement a
function of a prompt rather than of the circuit.

There are two addressees, following the regulation rather than convenience.
$\varphi_{\text{overseer}}$ is built on Annex IV 2(e) and 3 with Article 14(4)(c),
and keyed on the dominant layer band, then the size class, then the ranked input
segment. $\varphi_{\text{affected}}$ is built on Article 86(1) and leads with the
input segment, because the right is owed to the person the decision is about.
Three granularities are nested by construction, so a claim at a finer granularity
refines rather than contradicts the coarser one.

The choice of keys reflects what each addressee can act on. A human overseer
under Article 14 needs to know broadly where in the system a behaviour is
implemented and how concentrated that implementation is, because those are the
properties that determine whether monitoring or intervention at a particular point
is plausible. An affected person under Article 86 has no use for layer indices;
what they can understand and contest is which part of the input the decision
depended on. The map therefore produces different statements for the two
addressees from the same circuit, and both are derived mechanically.

A reviewer will ask whether the size bins were chosen to favour some conclusion.
They were returned by a committed calibration rule from a measured node-count
curve, not chosen by hand, and the rule is part of the pre-registered code. We
nevertheless regard the binning as a parameter whose sensitivity should be
reported by anyone using a map of this kind, and we recommend that sensitivity
analyses over alternative binnings, including equal-frequency bins and uniform
rescalings of the committed thresholds, accompany any use of $\varphi$ in
practice.

## 6 Method

#### Model and task.

GPT-2 small on indirect object identification
[15]. The choice is not an apology. The non-identifiability and
faithfulness literature this paper extends works at this scale, comparability is
the point, and the edge count is what makes a size-matched random baseline
meaningful.

#### Grid.

Seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four
corruption distributions nested within the five operators that read them, four
metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, five seeds: 1,540 discovery
cells and 18,480 specifications as pre-registered. Corruption is nested rather
than crossed because two ablation operators never read the corrupt distribution,
so crossing them would emit duplicate specifications. Discovery uses the edge
attribution patching family [14] and integrated edge gradients, as
implemented in the library released with Miller et al. [8]; the automated circuit
discovery lineage is Conmy et al. [2]. The four corruption levels are taken from
Wang et al. [15].

The grid is deliberately conservative in one respect: it contains only choices the
instrument implements. A wider literature review would add further operators and
objectives, and a provider is free to use any of them. The grid should therefore be
understood as a floor on the space a competent analyst might occupy, not a ceiling.

#### Pre-registration.

The analysis plan was committed and tagged before
the confirmatory sweep began, with alternative write-ups drafted in advance so that
no direction could be presented as a surprise. Deviations are recorded in an
append-only file with their dates and whether each was decided before or after the
affected result was seen.

#### Statistics.

No $p$ -value is computed across specifications anywhere.
Specifications are a designed grid, not an independent sample
[13, 12]. Where uncertainty is reported it comes from a nonparametric
bootstrap that resamples specifications, never pairs, at $B=10{,}000$ , because
pairwise statistics are U-statistics and pairs sharing a specification are
dependent. Intervals quantify uncertainty given the grid and license nothing
beyond it.

#### Two exclusions, criteria fixed before any circuit was seen.

Exclusion criteria were written into the pre-registration before any circuit was
inspected. A discovery cell that does not execute is recorded as a discard with
its cause and is not repaired: the library is the instrument under test and is
reproduced verbatim, so altering its code would change what is being studied.

The second exclusion is the metric-relative threshold rule. A specification
produces a claim only if its circuit reaches the pre-registered fraction of the
full model’s score under the specification’s own metric. Because the metrics differ
in how easily they are satisfied, this rule discards specifications unevenly across
metrics, and the surviving pool is therefore not balanced by design even though
the grid is. The unevenness was disclosed before the lock from a six-cell
validation slice. We report the composition of the surviving pool rather than
reweighting it, since any reweighting would itself be an analytic choice.

## 7 Results

The decision rules and thresholds used in this section were fixed and tagged
before the confirmatory sweep ran, and none was revisited. Because the purpose of
the paper is to set out a framework for documentation rather than to rank methods,
we organise the section around the questions a documentation reader would ask, and
around the analyses a provider would need to run to answer them.

### 7.1 Circuits are almost disjoint

The first question is structural: when two specifications in the grid each select a
circuit, how much do the circuits share? Equation 1 answers this directly, and with
the number of distinct circuits the grid produces the computation can be done
exactly over all pairs rather than sampled.

The distribution of pairwise distances is more informative than its mean. A small
number of near-identical pairs can coexist with a large mass of pairs that share
little, and the mean alone conceals which picture holds. We therefore recommend
reporting quantiles of $D$ alongside $\bar{J}$ , and reading both against the
analytic random line $k/(2|E|-k)$ for circuits of $k$ edges. That line is very
low for small circuits in a graph of this size and rises quickly with $k$ , so
beating chance is a weak standard at small sizes and a demanding one at large
sizes. Any statement that discovered circuits “agree” should be accompanied by the
size at which the agreement was measured.

### 7.2 The claim flips on three quarters of pairs

The second question is whether structural differences propagate to the statements
a documentation reader would see. The claim map exists precisely to make this
question answerable: two circuits can differ in many edges and still receive the
same statement, because $\varphi$ discards everything except the dominant layer
band, the size class and the ranked input segment.

The overseer map at medium granularity can produce nine combinations of layer
band and size class, and the affected-person map produces fewer at its coarsest
level. Inspecting which combinations are populated, and by which regions of the
grid, is the natural first step for any provider. A combination populated only by
specifications using one metric, or one ablation operator, tells the reader that
the statement depends on that choice; a combination populated evenly across the
grid tells the reader that it does not. The specification curve of Simonsohn et
al. [12] is a convenient display: specifications ordered by claim class in the
upper panel, with the active level of each axis marked beneath. The width of each
step is the share of the space that supports that statement.

Because the granularities are nested, this display can be produced at each level
of detail. A provider uncertain whether a fine-grained statement is supportable can
fall back to a coarser one and inspect the same display again. Whether the coarse
statement is adequate for the addressee is then a question about the regulation,
not about the circuit.

### 7.3 No analytic axis rescues the filing

A third question is practical: if statements depend on analytic choices, could a
standards body simply fix the most consequential choice? The within-group view
answers this. Conditioning on a single axis and comparing statements only within
each level of that axis shows how much of the dependence that axis carries.

Two cautions apply. First, the axes that most affect structure need not be the
axes that most affect the statement. A variance decomposition on the logarithm of
selected circuit size describes what drives structure, and the ablation operator,
the corruption distribution and their interaction are natural candidates there,
since they determine what the model sees when an edge is removed. The statement,
however, is keyed on layer band and input segment, which may respond to different
axes. A standards body reading only a structural decomposition could standardise
the wrong choice. Second, conditioning should weight every pair equally rather
than every group equally, so that small groups do not dominate the summary; this
is a detail, but it changes conclusions when group sizes are unequal, as they are
here because of the discard rule.

### 7.4 The result under maximum pressure

The most demanding version of the question strips every trace of circuit size from
the statement, leaving only the dominant layer band, and compares statements only
between circuits of the same size. This removes two routes by which statements
could differ for reasons unrelated to where the behaviour is implemented: the size
class itself, and correlations between size and layer band induced by the
threshold rule.

We recommend this control to anyone using a map of our kind, because it isolates
the component of the statement a human overseer would most naturally act on.
If the layer attribution is stable under this control, size-related variation in
the statement can be treated as a reporting detail. If it is not, the attribution
itself depends on analytic choices, and the documentation should say so.

### 7.5 The random baseline, and why its pooled direction misleads

A size-matched random null, drawing edge sets uniformly from the full
32,491-edge population at the sizes the grid actually selects, is the obvious
baseline for any comparison of discovered circuits. It is also a baseline whose
pooled behaviour is easy to misread.

The reason is degeneracy. Above roughly 1,000 edges a uniform draw touches all
156 components and therefore produces the same layer band and size class almost
every time. Pooled over sizes, the null then looks highly consistent, not because
random circuits agree on anything meaningful but because large random circuits
cannot be told apart by a coarse map. Any comparison between discovered circuits
and this null must therefore be made within size. Pooled comparisons conflate the
behaviour of the discovered circuits with the size distribution the threshold rule
happens to produce, and the direction of a pooled comparison can be the opposite of
the direction within every size stratum. This is a standard consequence of
aggregating over a variable that is an outcome of the specification rather than an
input to it, and we draw the general lesson in Section 9.

### 7.6 Filings differ more than mechanisms, over part of the range

The last question returns to the phantom specialisation objection. Two circuits
that receive different statements might nonetheless implement the same
computation, in which case the difference in statements reflects the vocabulary
of $\varphi$ rather than any difference a reader should care about.

The appropriate test is functional. For each pair of circuits, per-example correct
or incorrect verdicts on held-out prompts can be compared using the measures of
Bayat Makou et al. [1], reproduced verbatim. Raw agreement is not enough on its
own: two circuits that are each correct on most examples will agree on most
examples by chance alone, and raw agreement rises mechanically with accuracy.
Cohen’s kappa corrects for this and is the quantity that distinguishes circuits
that are right about the same examples from circuits that are merely right about
the same fraction of examples. We recommend reporting both, stratified by circuit
size, since accuracy and therefore chance agreement change substantially across
the size range.

If kappa is high, discovery is plausibly sampling from an equivalence class and
differing statements are a presentational issue. If kappa is near zero, the
circuits are functionally distinct and differing statements describe different
mechanisms. In either case, the comparison between statement-level and
function-level disagreement should be made within size, for the reasons set out
in Section 7.5.

## 8 The filability protocol

Reporting circuit-level evidence for documentation. For a filed
statement derived from a circuit:

1.

Declare the specification space $\mathcal{S}$ : the analytic axes and the
levels of each that a competent analyst could defend, each with a citation.

2.

Declare the claim map $\varphi$ as deterministic, published code. Not a
language model.

3.

Report the distribution of statements produced across $\mathcal{S}$ , not only
the statement produced by the analyst’s preferred specification.

4.

Report the discard rate per axis level, and the composition of the surviving
pool.

5.

Report every pooled statistic alongside its within-group decomposition, and in
particular its decomposition by circuit size.

A filing that cannot describe the space it was drawn from has not been audited. It
has been asserted. The protocol does not require the regulator to adjudicate which
analytic choice is correct, which is the property that makes it implementable: it
requires only that the filer declare the space and report how the statement
behaves within it. A receiving body can then set its own tolerance for dependence
on analytic choices, and can tighten or loosen that tolerance as practice matures,
without any change to what filers are asked to disclose.

## 9 Limitations

#### One model, one task.

Larger models have more components, so both the
layer band and the size class have more room, and how the statements behave at
scale is not obvious. This is the limitation most likely to change any conclusion
drawn from the design.

A second-model replication is pre-registered but not yet run: a 924-cell grid on
Pythia-160m, a model of a different architecture family that performs the same
task, identical on every axis except that the seed axis carries three levels
rather than five. The analysis plan, the reduced grid, and the criteria for what
would count as replication rather than refutation are committed and timestamped
before any cell of it ran. It will be reported in a revision in whichever
direction it falls. A second task remains designed and not run.

#### Circuit size is an outcome, not an axis.

It is chosen by the threshold
rule, not by the analyst, and it is correlated with several of the pre-registered
axes. Any pooled quantity computed across specifications therefore mixes the
behaviour of interest with the size distribution those specifications induce. We
take this to be a general hazard for multiverse designs whose specifications select
objects of different sizes, and we recommend that every pooled statistic be
reported with its within-size decomposition.

#### The multiverse is as wide as the library, not the literature.

Optimal
ablation [5] is a defensible operator the instrument does not
implement, so it never entered the space. Any dependence on analytic choice
measured within this grid is therefore a lower bound with respect to the field’s
full set of defensible choices.

#### The discard rate is high and uneven.

The surviving pool is metric
imbalanced. The threshold rule was fixed in advance and no failing item was
repaired, but the composition is a property of the reported set and we state it
rather than adjust for it.

#### The bootstrap is invalid for one reported family.

Where
conditioning groups hold only two to five specifications, retained self-pairs
dominate and bootstrap intervals are unusable; such quantities should be reported
as point estimates with the diagnostic attached. We did not construct a
bias-corrected estimator in response to this, because choosing an estimator in
response to a result is the behaviour this paper is concerned with.

## 10 Discussion

#### What standardising one axis buys.

It is tempting to treat analytic dependence as a problem with a single cause
and a single fix: identify the most consequential choice, standardise it, and
proceed. The structure of the grid makes this unlikely. Seven axes, each with a
published rationale, interact through the threshold rule and through circuit size,
and the axes that govern structure need not be the axes that govern the statement.
A procedure that standardises one axis and declares the problem solved should be
asked to show the within-group view that justifies the declaration.

#### On the instrument.

The tooling that regulatory evidence would rest on is
young. We use it verbatim, because the alternative would be to study our own
modifications rather than the instrument a provider would actually run, and we
record every execution failure as a discard with its cause. This is not a criticism
of a library whose authors are among those calling for the field to address exactly
these questions [10]; it is an observation that documentation practice should
assume the tooling will continue to change, and should record which version
produced which evidence.

#### What a regulator can take from this.

Not that interpretability
evidence is worthless, but that its evidentiary weight is a property that can be
examined rather than assumed, and that the examination is cheap relative to the
sweep that produced the circuit in the first place. The analysis layer described
here runs without a GPU once circuits are discovered. Asking a provider to declare
the specification space and report how its statement behaves within that space
adds little to the cost of producing the evidence and a great deal to the ability
of anyone else to check it.

## 11 Reproducibility

The pre-registration is a timestamped commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory
in the public repository, made before the confirmatory sweep began. Every reported
number traces to a config, a seed and an environment fingerprint.
The confirmatory sweep ran under a single environment across all discovery cells,
verified from the results archive rather than asserted, and the code commit was
recovered by content-addressed comparison of the uploaded archive against the git
tree, 22 of 22 files identical. The analysis layer runs without a GPU.

A verification script recomputes every reported quantity from raw results and
asserts against what is reported, including brute-force pairwise checks of every
pairwise statistic. A second script checks that every numeric token in this
manuscript matches a value derived from the stored results. The claim map, the
size-bin calibration rule and the edge-count derivation are published as code with
their own tests. The test suite is 343 tests.

# Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability

Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation

Ajay Pravin Mahale

12 August 2026

###### Abstract

The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to file technical
documentation describing how the system reaches its decisions. Circuit discovery,
the most developed instrument of mechanistic interpretability, is a candidate
source of that content. We test it under inter-analyst variation: the same system
and tool, different defensible settings.

We pre-registered a crossed grid of seven analytic axes, every level taken from a
published implementation, and mapped each discovered circuit through a
deterministic claim map $\varphi$ to a structured Annex IV statement. Across 15,840
pre-registered specifications on GPT-2 small and the indirect object
identification task, of which 7,561 produced a claim, the derived statement
flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725 to 0.738) and the modal
claim commands 41.1% of the space. Filability fails at every pre-registered
tolerance.

Standardising the evaluation metric leaves the flip rate at 59.4%. With circuit
size removed from the claim and held fixed, it is 27.1% (95% CI 0.255 to 0.286),
above the pre-registered threshold. Median pairwise Jaccard overlap is 4% and
Cohen's kappa on per-example verdicts is 0.015.

We give the filability criterion as a standalone protocol, and report that one
of the seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library's
own canonical task. The study covers one model and one task; behaviour at scale
is untested.

## 1 Introduction

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to file
technical documentation. Annex IV point 2(b) asks for "the general logic of the
AI system and of the algorithms". Point 2(e) asks for "an assessment of the
technical measures needed to facilitate the interpretation of the outputs".
Article 86(1) gives a person subject to certain automated decisions the right to
"clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the
decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken". Text is
quoted from the consolidated version as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744,
CELEX 02024R1689-20260727, read 11 August 2026.

Circuit discovery returns a subgraph attributed to a behaviour and has the most
mature tooling in the field. We quantify the displacement of the resulting
regulatory claim over the space of defensible analytic specifications and attach
a decision rule usable by a standards body. No new discovery method is proposed,
and no claim is made that interpretability lacks value; the claim concerns the
evidentiary status of circuit-level evidence as currently produced.

#### Contributions.

(i) A pre-registered multiverse over seven analytic axes of circuit discovery,
with every level drawn from a published implementation, and a deterministic map
from circuits to Annex IV statements.
(ii) A filability criterion, $\pi^{*}\geq 1-\alpha$ , applicable within a
conformity procedure, with its measured value on a canonical task.
(iii) Persistence of the instability under single-axis standardisation, removal
of circuit size from the claim, and conditioning on size.
(iv) Three pooled statistics of ours that invert under within-size
decomposition, a hazard for multiverse designs in which specifications select
objects of differing size.

## 2 Related work

#### Non-identifiability.

Méloux et al. [6] show that, under mechanistic interpretability's own criteria, a
behaviour need not admit a unique explanation. We take this as premise and
measure its cost at the point of filing.

#### Faithfulness metric sensitivity.

Miller et al. [8] find ablation-based faithfulness scores highly sensitive to
seemingly insignificant design changes, reflecting methodological choice as well
as the circuit. We cross seven axes rather than one and propagate to a regulatory
statement. Their released library is our instrument, so the study evaluates the
tooling on its own definitions.

#### Structure versus function.

Bayat Makou et al. [1] vary input statistics at fixed task and find structurally
distinct circuits implementing the same computation (phantom specialisation).
Applied here, discovery would sample an equivalence class of behaviourally
identical subgraphs, and a flip rate over claims would index the sampled member.
Section 7.6 tests this functionally; our circuits are not functionally
interchangeable.

#### Variance as estimation.

Méloux et al. [7] analyse mechanistic interpretability as statistical estimation
and study estimator variance. Seed is one axis of our space; we work at the level
of the full specification.

#### Auditability.

Lan et al. [4] document two papers reaching conflicting conclusions about one
behaviour, with a third finding both partly correct and incomparable, and call for
auditing standards enabling certification in safety-critical settings. We supply
a measurement and a criterion. Sharkey et al. [10] list open problems including
socio-technical ones; Mueller et al. [9] argue cross-method comparison requires
standardised evaluation, adjacent to standardised specification as a precondition
for certification.

#### Multiverse method.

The design follows Steegen et al. [13], and the specification curve of
Simonsohn et al. [12] is adapted for visualisation. Simmons et al. [11] identify
undisclosed analytic flexibility as sufficient to present almost anything as
significant; stability of an explanation is a claim of that type.

#### Explanation metrics under optimisation pressure.

Hsia et al. [3] show sufficiency and comprehensiveness can be inflated without
changing predictions or explanations. Both are among our four evaluation metrics,
and discard rates are reported per metric.

## 3 What this paper is not claiming

Discovered circuits are not equivalent to random: at fixed circuit size they are
more stable than a size-matched random null, 0.2746 against 0.4230.

Filings do not differ where mechanisms coincide: functional instability is 0.3972
pooled and 0.4777 at the smallest circuits.

Discovery does not return a single mechanism under varying description: Cohen's
kappa is 0.0146.

Seeds are not the source: the seed selects sampled prompts, i.e. evaluation-set
variability rather than nondeterminism.

No claim is made about scale. One model, one task.

## 4 Formalism

A specification is $s=(o,a,d,m,\tau,P,r,g)$ , with $o$ the discovery objective,
$a$ the ablation operator, $d$ the corruption distribution, $m$ the evaluation
metric, $\tau$ the size threshold, $P$ the prompt variant, $r$ the seed and $g$
the granularity. Every level of every axis is taken from a published
implementation; none was introduced for this study.

Discovery returns $C(s)\subseteq E$ . For GPT-2 small under the factorised graph
with separate query, key and value inputs, $|E|=32{,}491$ , confirmed from the

MLP $b$ receives from those sources plus its own block's heads, and the output
receives from all 157 non-terminal sources. Components are drawn from 144 attention
heads and 12 MLPs, 156 in total.

## 8 The filability protocol

Filability of an interpretability claim. For a filed claim $c$
derived from a circuit:

1.

Declare the specification space $\mathcal{S}$ : the analytic axes and the
levels of each that a competent analyst could defend, each with a citation.

2.

Declare the claim map $\varphi$ as deterministic, published code. Not a
language model.

3.

Compute $\pi^{*}=\max_{c}n_{c}/N$ over $\mathcal{S}$ , and $F$ by
Equation 2.

4.

The claim is filable at tolerance $\alpha$ if $\pi^{*}\geq 1-\alpha$ .

5.

Report $\pi^{*}$ , $F$ , the discard rate per axis level, and the
within-group decomposition of any pooled statistic.

The protocol requires declaration of the space and the agreeing share, not
adjudication of the correct analytic choice.

## 9 Limitations

#### One model, one task.

Larger models give both layer band and size class more room; the sign of the
effect on $F$ is not determined.

A second-model replication is pre-registered but not yet run: a 924-cell grid on
Pythia-160m, a different architecture family performing the same task, identical
on every axis except a seed axis of three levels rather than five. The plan, the
reduced grid, and replication-versus-refutation criteria are committed and
timestamped before any cell ran, and will be reported in a revision in either
direction. A second task is designed and not run.

#### Circuit size is an outcome, not an axis.

It is selected by the threshold rule and distorts three pooled quantities: $F$ ,
the direction of the null comparison, and the sign of the functional gap.
Conditioning on it drops $F$ from 0.7316 to 0.2746, more than standardising any
pre-registered axis. Every pooled statistic is reported with its within-size
decomposition.

#### The multiverse is as wide as the library, not the literature.

Optimal ablation [5] is defensible but unimplemented in the instrument, so the
measured $F$ is a lower bound over the field's defensible choices.

#### The discard rate is high and uneven.

52.3%, with a metric-imbalanced surviving pool. The rule was fixed in advance and
no failing item repaired; composition is stated, not adjusted.

#### The bootstrap is invalid for one reported family.

Where conditioning groups hold two to five specifications, retained self-pairs
dominate and intervals are unusable; those quantities are point estimates with the
diagnostic attached. No bias-corrected estimator was constructed post hoc, since
estimator selection conditional on a result is the behaviour under study.

## 10 Discussion

#### What standardising one axis buys.

The metric removes 0.1377 of a 0.7316 flip rate; no single axis suffices.

#### On the instrument.

One of seven documented, publicly exported discovery objectives does not run on
the library's own canonical task. It is reported as a discard with its rate, as an
observation on tooling maturity, not as criticism of authors who are among those
calling for this to be addressed [10].

#### What a regulator can take from this.

Evidentiary weight of interpretability evidence is a measurable property, and the
measurement is cheap relative to the sweep producing the circuit.

## 11 Reproducibility

The pre-registration is a timestamped commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory in the
public repository, made before the confirmatory sweep. Every reported number
traces to a config, a seed and an environment fingerprint. The sweep ran under a
single environment across all 1,320 cells, verified from the results archive, and
the code commit was recovered by content-addressed comparison of the uploaded
archive against the git tree, 22 of 22 files identical. The analysis layer runs
without a GPU.

A verification script recomputes every headline quantity from raw results: 36
checks, 0 failures, with $F$ derived by three routes including brute-force
pairwise computation. A second script checks every numeric token in this
manuscript against values derived from stored results. Tables are emitted
directly from results. The test suite is 343 tests.

# Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability

Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation

Ajay Pravin Mahale

12 August 2026

###### Abstract

The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to file technical
documentation describing how the system reaches its decisions. Mechanistic
interpretability is the obvious source of such evidence, and circuit discovery is
its most developed instrument. We ask what it would take for that evidence to be
relied upon under the condition that regulation presumes: two competent analysts,
the same system, the same tool, different defensible settings.

We set out a pre-registered crossed grid of analytic axes for circuit discovery,
with every level taken from a published implementation, and apply it to GPT-2
small on the indirect object identification task. We describe how the grid was
constructed, why each axis belongs in it, how the levels were sourced, and how
the resulting circuits relate to the language of Annex IV and Article 86. We
argue that the space of defensible choices in circuit discovery is wide enough,
and the choices consequential enough, that a filed circuit-level account cannot
be read without knowing where in that space it was produced.

We propose a disclosure protocol under which a filer declares the specification
space alongside the evidence, and we discuss what conformity assessment bodies
can and cannot reasonably demand of interpretability tooling in its current
state. The study covers one model and one task, and whether the considerations
raised here change at scale is untested.

## 1 Introduction

An audit means two auditors reach the same conclusion. That is not a definition
borrowed from machine learning; it is what makes an audit worth commissioning.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to file
technical documentation. Annex IV point 2(b) asks for “the general logic of the
AI system and of the algorithms”. Point 2(e) asks for “an assessment of the
technical measures needed to facilitate the interpretation of the outputs”.
Article 86(1) gives a person subject to certain automated decisions the right to
“clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the
decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken”. These are
quoted from the consolidated text as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744,
CELEX 02024R1689-20260727, read 11 August 2026.

Mechanistic interpretability offers to supply the technical content. Circuit
discovery produces a subgraph said to explain a behaviour, and it is the part of
the field with mature tooling. If a provider files a circuit-level account of why
its system behaved as it did, the filing is worth something only if a second
analyst, given the same system and the same tool, would file something compatible.

That condition is rarely examined directly. Circuit discovery papers typically
report one configuration, chosen for reasons that are sensible but not
mandatory: a particular ablation operator, a particular corruption distribution,
a particular faithfulness metric, a particular threshold. Each of these has
published alternatives that a competent analyst could defend. A regulator
reading a filing has no way to know which of those alternatives were tried, and
no way to know whether the account would read differently under them.

This paper takes the analytic flexibility of circuit discovery seriously as a
regulatory problem. We do not propose a better circuit discovery method, and we
do not argue that interpretability is worthless. We argue that the evidence, as
currently produced and reported, does not carry the information that filing it
presumes, and that the missing information is the specification space within
which a given circuit was obtained.

#### Contributions.

(i) A pre-registered multiverse design over seven analytic axes of circuit
discovery, with every level drawn from a published implementation.
(ii) An account of how the outputs of circuit discovery relate to the specific
documentation obligations of Annex IV and Article 86, and of the two distinct
addressees those obligations imply.
(iii) A disclosure protocol that a conformity procedure could require without
having to adjudicate which analytic choice is correct.
(iv) A discussion of methodological hazards in multiverse designs whose
specifications select objects of different sizes.

## 2 Related work

#### Non-identifiability.

Méloux et al. [6] ask whether, for a given
behaviour and under mechanistic interpretability’s own criteria, a unique
explanation exists, and answer that it need not. Our premise is theirs. Our
contribution is downstream: we ask what non-identifiability implies when an
explanation is filed rather than published.

#### Faithfulness metric sensitivity.

Miller et al. [8] survey design
choices in ablation-based faithfulness measurement and find existing methods
highly sensitive to seemingly insignificant changes, concluding that faithfulness
scores reflect the researcher’s methodological choices as well as the circuit.
They establish that one axis matters. We consider seven together, and frame the
question in terms of a regulatory statement. Their released library is the
instrument we use, which means our design is a stress test of the tooling by the
tooling’s own definitions.

#### Structure versus function.

Bayat Makou et al. [1] vary input
statistics while holding the task fixed and find that structurally distinct
circuits implement the same computation, a pattern they term phantom
specialisation. This is an important consideration for any study of variation
across discovered circuits: if discovery merely samples from an equivalence class
of behaviourally identical subgraphs, structural differences between circuits
need not correspond to differences in what a filing should say. We return to this
in Section 7.6.

#### Variance as estimation.

Méloux et al. [7] treat mechanistic
interpretability as statistical estimation and analyse the variance of the
estimator. Seed variance is one axis of our space; their framing is the natural
statistical companion to what we do at the level of the whole specification.

#### Auditability.

Lan et al. [4] observe that two papers reached
conflicting conclusions about the same behaviour, with a third finding both partly
correct and incomparable, and call for auditing standards so that findings can be
certified in safety-critical settings. We take that call as our starting point.
Sharkey et al. [10] list open problems in the field, including the socio-technical
ones this paper touches, and Mueller et al. [9] argue that comparison across
methods requires standardised evaluation, which is adjacent to our argument that
certification requires declared specification.

#### Multiverse method.

The design follows Steegen et al. [13], who propose
reporting results across the space of defensible data-processing choices, and
Simonsohn et al. [12], whose specification curve is the natural visualisation for
such designs. Simmons et al. [11] named the underlying problem: undisclosed
flexibility in analysis lets an analyst present almost anything as significant.
We are applying a psychology methods literature to a machine learning evidentiary
question, and the transfer is not decorative. The claim that an explanation is
stable is exactly the kind of claim that undisclosed flexibility can manufacture.

#### Explanation metrics under optimisation pressure.

Hsia et al. [3] show that sufficiency and comprehensiveness can be inflated
without changing predictions or explanations. Two of our four evaluation metrics
are those two, which is one reason we treat the metric as an analytic axis in its
own right rather than as a neutral measuring device.

## 3 What this paper is not claiming

Stated early because each is a reading the argument does not support.

We are not claiming that discovered circuits are no better than random. Nothing
in the design or discussion here bears on whether circuit discovery recovers
genuine structure; the literature gives good reason to think it often does.

Nor that interpretability evidence should be excluded from technical
documentation. Our argument concerns what must accompany it, not whether it
belongs.

Nor that discovery methods are defective. The variation we discuss arises from
choices that are each legitimate, and the tooling exposes them precisely because
the field has not settled them.

Nor that random seeds are the main concern. The seed here selects which prompts
are sampled, so it is evaluation-set variability rather than nondeterminism, and
it is one axis among seven.

And nothing at all about scale. One model, one task.

## 4 Formalism

A specification is a tuple of analytic choices covering the discovery objective,
the ablation operator, the corruption distribution, the evaluation metric, the
size threshold, the prompt variant, the seed and the granularity of the
resulting description. Every level of every axis is taken from a published
implementation. None was invented for this study.

Circuit discovery returns a subset of the model’s edge set. For GPT-2 small
under the factorised graph with separate query, key and value inputs, the edge
set runs to tens of thousands of edges, and circuits touch components drawn from
the attention heads and MLP blocks across all twelve layers. The size of this
space matters for interpretation: a circuit of a few hundred edges is a very
small fraction of the graph, and the number of distinct subgraphs of that size is
astronomically large.

#### Circuit instability.

Two circuits obtained under different specifications can be compared
structurally, by the edges they share, or functionally, by whether they succeed
and fail on the same inputs. These are distinct questions. Structural difference
need not imply functional difference, as Bayat Makou et al. [1] document, and
functional agreement in aggregate need not imply agreement on individual
examples. Any study that compares circuits across specifications should keep the
two notions apart.

#### Claim instability.

A regulator does not read edge lists. What is filed is a statement in natural
language, constrained by the documentation obligation it answers. The relevant
question for filing is therefore not whether two circuits share edges but
whether they support compatible statements of the kind Annex IV and Article 86
require. This shifts the unit of analysis from the circuit to the statement
derived from it, and makes the procedure by which a statement is derived part of
the evidence.

#### Filability.

We use the term informally for the property a filed account must have if a
second competent analyst, working within the declared space of defensible
choices, would be expected to reach a compatible account. The term names a
standard rather than a measurement; how a conformity procedure might
operationalise it is discussed in Section 8.

## 5 The claim map

Any bridge from circuits to regulatory statements is open to attack, so the
choices involved should be fixed in advance, implemented as deterministic code
where possible, and published. A language model should not be used to generate
the statements; doing so would introduce model variance on top of circuit
variance with no way to separate them.

There are two addressees, following the regulation rather than convenience. The
overseer, addressed by Annex IV 2(e) and 3 together with Article 14(4)(c), needs
an account of where in the model the behaviour is carried and how concentrated
the responsible computation is. The affected person, addressed by Article 86(1),
needs an account of which parts of the input drove the decision, because the
right is owed to the person the decision is about. These lead with different
information, and a statement adequate for one addressee may be inadequate for
the other.

Statements can also be framed at different granularities. A coarse statement
might say only which region of the network is responsible; a finer one might add
how distributed the computation is and which input segment it reads. Nesting the
granularities, so that a finer statement refines rather than contradicts a
coarser one, keeps the hierarchy interpretable and allows a filer to choose the
level of detail appropriate to the addressee.

A reviewer will ask how size categories, if used, are chosen. Our view is that
any such categories should be returned by a committed calibration rule from a
measured curve rather than selected by hand, and that sensitivity to the choice
should be reported. The general principle is that every discretisation between
circuit and statement is itself an analytic choice, and belongs in the declared
specification space.

## 6 Method

#### Model and task.

GPT-2 small on indirect object identification
[15]. The choice is not an apology. The non-identifiability and
faithfulness literature this paper extends works at this scale, comparability is
the point, and the modest size of the graph makes exhaustive analysis of the
design tractable.

#### Grid.

Seven discovery objectives, seven ablation operators, four
corruption distributions nested within the five operators that read them, four
metrics, three thresholds, two prompt variants, five seeds: 1,540 discovery
cells and 18,480 specifications as pre-registered. Corruption is nested rather
than crossed because two ablation operators never read the corrupt distribution,
so crossing them would emit duplicate specifications. Discovery uses the edge
attribution patching family [14] and integrated edge gradients, as
implemented in the library released with Miller et al. [8]; the automated circuit
discovery lineage is Conmy et al. [2]. The four corruption levels are taken from
Wang et al. [15].

#### Pre-registration.

The analysis plan was committed and tagged before
any confirmatory work began. Deviations are recorded in an append-only file with
their dates and whether each was decided before or after the affected material
was seen. Pre-registration matters especially here: a study about analytic
flexibility that was itself analytically flexible would undermine its own
argument.

#### Statistics.

No $p$ -value is appropriate across specifications. Specifications
are a designed grid, not an independent sample [13, 12]. Any
uncertainty quantification over such a grid should resample specifications rather
than pairs of specifications, because pairwise quantities are dependent whenever
pairs share a specification, and any interval obtained should be read as
conditional on the grid rather than as licensing inference beyond it.

#### Two exclusions, criteria fixed before any circuit was seen.

The pre-registration fixes in advance how cells that fail to execute, and
specifications for which the threshold rule admits no circuit, are to be
handled: both are recorded as discards with their rates, and neither is repaired.
The library is the instrument under test and is reproduced verbatim. Because a
metric-relative threshold rule can admit circuits at different rates for
different metrics, the composition of the surviving pool may differ from the
balanced composition of the design, and that composition should be reported
rather than smoothed.

## 7 Results

This section works through the questions the design is built to address, in the
order a conformity assessment body would plausibly raise them. Throughout, we
emphasise what each question requires of the analysis and what an answer could
and could not establish.

### 7.1 Circuits are almost disjoint

The first question is structural: do specifications that differ only in
defensible analytic choices return overlapping sets of edges? The literature on
non-identifiability [6] and faithfulness sensitivity [8] gives reason to
expect substantial variation, and inspection of circuits across our grid is
consistent with that expectation.

Two cautions apply to any structural comparison. First, overlap must be read
against chance. In a graph of this size, two random subsets of a few hundred
edges are expected to share almost nothing, so exceeding chance overlap is a
weak bar. Second, structural overlap is not the quantity a filing depends on.
Two circuits with little edge overlap may still support the same statement, and
two with considerable overlap may not. Structural variation is a premise for the
regulatory question, not an answer to it.

### 7.2 The claim flips on three quarters of pairs

The regulatory question concerns statements. Mapping circuits through a fixed
procedure to statements of the kind Annex IV asks for exposes something the edge
view conceals: statements derived from different specifications can disagree not
only in emphasis but in substance, for example in which region of the network
they hold responsible for the behaviour.

This is the scenario regulation is least equipped to handle. A provider choosing
among defensible configurations could, in such a case, file a statement whose
opposite another analyst could equally defend, and nothing in the filing would
reveal this. The difficulty does not depend on fine-grained statement language:
even the coarsest account available to an affected person rests on choices that
the filing does not disclose.

A specification curve, ordering specifications by the statement they support and
displaying which analytic levels are active for each, is the natural way to
present this to a reviewer. It makes visible both the share of the space
supporting any given statement and whether particular analytic levels are
associated with particular statements.

### 7.3 No analytic axis rescues the filing

A natural response to analytic variation is to standardise. If one axis is
responsible for most of the disagreement, a standard could fix it and leave the
rest to the analyst. The design allows each axis to be held fixed in turn, with
comparisons made within its levels rather than across them.

Two considerations suggest caution about this route. The evaluation metric is
the obvious candidate, given the sensitivity documented by Miller et al. [8]
and the inflation results of Hsia et al. [3], but standardising it completely
would be more than a conformity procedure could reasonably demand, and would
still leave six axes free. More subtly, the axes that govern circuit structure
need not be the axes that govern the derived statement. A standards body that
reasoned from structural variation alone might standardise the axis that most
changes the edge set and leave untouched the axis that most changes what is
filed. Decisions about standardisation should be made at the level of the
statement.

### 7.4 The result under maximum pressure

The most aggressive control available is to remove from the statement anything
that depends on circuit size and to compare only specifications whose circuits
have the same size. What remains is the attribution of the behaviour to a region
of the model, the core of an Annex IV 2(b) account of the system’s general logic.

This control matters because size is the most obvious channel through which
analytic choices could alter a statement without altering the substance of the
mechanism described. If disagreement persists once size is held fixed and
removed from the statement, it cannot be attributed to that channel. A filing
that rests on where in the model a behaviour is located should be able to
withstand this test.

### 7.5 The random baseline, and why its pooled direction misleads

Any study of this kind needs a baseline: random edge subsets of matched size,
drawn from the full edge set and passed through the same procedure. The baseline
answers whether discovered circuits behave differently from arbitrary subgraphs.

Pooled comparisons against such a baseline are hazardous. At large circuit sizes
a uniform random draw touches every component of the model and can support only
one statement, so the baseline becomes degenerate in exactly the region where
discovered circuits may still vary. A pooled comparison then mixes the two
distributions of circuit size and can point in either direction for reasons
unrelated to the quality of discovery. The fair comparison is within size. We
regard any pooled baseline result reported without its within-size counterpart
as uninterpretable.

### 7.6 Filings differ more than mechanisms, over part of the range

The phantom specialisation objection [1] holds that structurally distinct
circuits may implement the same computation, in which case disagreement among
statements would reflect only which member of an equivalence class was sampled.
Addressing it requires a functional measurement rather than an argument.

The appropriate measurement compares, example by example, whether two circuits
succeed and fail on the same inputs, using the measures of Bayat Makou et al.
[1]. Raw agreement is not sufficient. Two circuits that are each correct on a
similar fraction of examples will agree on many examples by chance, so agreement
must be corrected for what accuracy alone would produce, for example with Cohen’s
kappa. Only chance-corrected agreement distinguishes circuits that implement the
same mechanism from circuits that are merely similarly accurate.

The relationship between statement disagreement and functional disagreement can
also vary with circuit size. Where mechanisms differ more than statements do, the
statement procedure is coarser than the mechanisms; where statements differ more
than mechanisms do, the procedure is amplifying differences that the mechanisms
do not carry. Both are informative, and a pooled figure can hide which regime
dominates in which part of the range.

## 8 The filability protocol

Disclosure of an interpretability claim. For a filed claim derived from a
circuit:

1.

Declare the specification space: the analytic axes and the levels of each that a
competent analyst could defend, each with a citation.

2.

Declare the procedure that maps a circuit to the filed statement as
deterministic, published code. Not a language model.

3.

State which specification produced the filed circuit, and why that
specification was selected.

4.

Report the discard rate per axis level, so that the composition of the evidence
is visible.

5.

Report any pooled statistic together with its within-group decomposition,
in particular within circuit size.

A filing that cannot state the space within which its evidence was produced has
not been audited. It has been asserted. The protocol does not require the
regulator to adjudicate which analytic choice is correct, which is the property
that makes it implementable: it requires only that the filer declare the space
and the choice made within it, so that a second analyst could reproduce or
challenge the account on equal terms.

The protocol is deliberately modest. It asks for nothing that a careful
interpretability paper should not already report, and it can be satisfied with
existing tooling. Its value lies in making explicit, as a condition of filing,
information that is currently optional and frequently omitted.

## 9 Limitations

#### One model, one task.

Larger models have more components, so both the space of possible circuits and
the space of possible statements are larger, and it is not obvious in which
direction the considerations raised here would move. This is the limitation most
likely to matter.

A second-model replication is pre-registered: a 924-cell grid on Pythia-160m, a
model of a different architecture family that performs the same task, identical
on every axis except that the seed axis carries three levels rather than five.
The analysis plan, the reduced grid, and the criteria for what would count as
replication rather than refutation are committed and timestamped in advance. A
second task remains designed and not run.

#### Circuit size is an outcome, not an axis.

It is chosen by the threshold rule rather than set by the analyst, and it can
therefore act as a hidden channel through which analytic choices propagate. We
take this to be a general hazard for multiverse designs whose specifications
select objects of different sizes, and recommend that every pooled statistic in
such designs be reported with its within-size decomposition.

#### The multiverse is as wide as the library, not the literature.

Optimal
ablation [5] is a defensible operator the instrument does not
implement, so it never entered the space. Any conclusion drawn from the grid is
therefore conservative with respect to the field’s full set of defensible
choices.

#### The discard rule shapes the evidence.

A metric-relative threshold rule may admit circuits unevenly across metrics. The
rule was fixed in advance and no failing item is to be repaired, but the
composition of the surviving set is a property of the reported evidence and
should be stated rather than adjusted for.

#### Resampling can fail for small groups.

Where conditioning groups hold only a handful of specifications, bootstrap
intervals for within-group quantities become unreliable. Such quantities are
better reported as point estimates with diagnostics attached. Constructing a
bias-corrected estimator in response to an unwelcome interval would be the
behaviour this paper warns against.

## 10 Discussion

#### What standardising one axis buys.

Less than it appears. The literature identifies several consequential choices
in circuit discovery, and there is no reason to expect any single one to account
for most of the variation in what is filed. A procedure that standardises one
axis and declares the problem solved would be relying on an assumption it has not
checked.

#### On the instrument.

Interpretability tooling is young, and a library that exposes many discovery
objectives and operators is doing the field a service by making the space of
choices explicit. Robustness of every exported configuration on every canonical
task cannot be taken for granted, and a filing that rests on such tooling should
record which configurations ran and which did not. This is not a criticism of
libraries whose authors are among those calling for the field to address exactly
this [10].

#### What a regulator can take from this.

Not that interpretability evidence is worthless, but that its evidentiary weight
depends on information that filings do not currently contain: the space of
defensible choices and the position of the filed evidence within it. Requiring
that information is cheap relative to the sweep that produced the circuit in the
first place, and it converts an assumed property into one that can be examined.

## 11 Reproducibility

The pre-registration is a timestamped commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory
in the public repository. Every configuration traces to a config, a seed and an
environment fingerprint. The grid is run under a single pinned environment, and
the code commit is recoverable by content-addressed comparison of archived
outputs against the git tree. The analysis layer runs without a GPU.

A verification script recomputes quantities from raw outputs and asserts against
what is reported, with pairwise quantities derived by more than one route
including a brute-force computation. A second script checks that every numeric
token in this manuscript matches a value derived from stored outputs. The test
suite is 343 tests.

###### Abstract

The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to file technical

circuit-level evidence is invariant to the choice among defensible settings when
the system and tool are held fixed.

published implementation, and passed each discovered circuit through a
deterministic claim map $\varphi$ to a structured Annex IV statement. Across 15,840
pre-registered specifications on GPT-2 small and indirect object identification,

specification pairs (95% CI 0.725 to 0.738), and the modal claim holds 41.1% of

plausibly accept.

and Cohen’s kappa is 0.015.

canonical task. The study covers one model and one task; scale is untested.

## 1 Introduction

An audit means two auditors reach the same conclusion; that property, not a
borrowed machine learning definition, is what an audit is commissioned for.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to file

AI system and of the algorithms”. Point 2(e) asks for “an assessment of the
technical measures needed to facilitate the interpretation of the outputs”.

decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken”. Quotations

CELEX 02024R1689-20260727, read 11 August 2026.

Circuit discovery returns a subgraph said to explain a behaviour and has the most
mature tooling in mechanistic interpretability. A circuit-level account filed by a
provider presupposes that a second analyst, given the same system and tool, would
file a compatible one.

We quantify the displacement of a regulatory claim over the space of defensible
analytic specifications and attach a decision rule usable by a standards body. We
propose no new discovery method and make no claim that interpretability is
worthless; the claim is that current evidence does not meet the standard filing

#### Contributions.

(i) A pre-registered multiverse over seven analytic axes of circuit discovery,
with every level drawn from a published implementation, and a deterministic map
from circuits to Annex IV statements.
(ii) A filability criterion, $\pi^{*}\geq 1-\alpha$ , applicable in a conformity
procedure, with its measured value on a canonical task.
(iii) Persistence of the instability under single-axis standardisation, removal of
circuit size from the claim, and conditioning on size.

sizes, pooled statistics can invert; three of ours do.

#### Non-identifiability.

Méloux et al. [6] ask whether a unique
explanation of a behaviour exists under mechanistic interpretability’s own
criteria, and find that it need not. We adopt the premise and measure its cost when
an explanation is filed rather than published.

#### Faithfulness metric sensitivity.

Miller et al. [8] survey design
choices in ablation-based faithfulness measurement, find high sensitivity to
seemingly insignificant changes, and conclude that faithfulness scores reflect
methodological choices as well as the circuit. They establish one axis; we cross
seven and propagate to a regulatory statement. Their released library is our
instrument, so the study is a stress test of the tooling under its own definitions.

#### Structure versus function.

Bayat Makou et al. [1] vary input
statistics at fixed task and find structurally distinct circuits implementing the
same computation, termed phantom specialisation. Under that reading, a flip rate
over claims would index which member of a behavioural equivalence class was
sampled. Section 7.6 tests this functionally; our circuits are not functionally
interchangeable.

#### Variance as estimation.

Méloux et al. [7] treat mechanistic
interpretability as statistical estimation and analyse estimator variance. Seed
variance is one of our axes; their framing is the statistical companion at the
level of the full specification.

#### Auditability.

Lan et al. [4] note two papers with conflicting conclusions about one
behaviour, a third finding both partly correct and incomparable, and call for
auditing standards to certify findings in safety-critical settings. We supply a
measurement and a criterion. Sharkey et al. [10] list open problems including
socio-technical ones, and Mueller et al. [9] argue that cross-method comparison
requires standardised evaluation, adjacent to our position that certification
requires standardised specification.

#### Multiverse method.

The design follows Steegen et al. [13] on reporting across defensible
data-processing choices and adapts the specification curve of
Simonsohn et al. [12]. Simmons et al. [11] showed that undisclosed analytic
flexibility lets almost anything be presented as significant; stability of an
explanation is a claim of exactly that type.

#### Explanation metrics under optimisation pressure.

Hsia et al. [3] show that sufficiency and comprehensiveness can be inflated
without changing predictions or explanations. Both are among our four evaluation
metrics, so discard rates are reported per metric rather than pooled.

Filings do not differ where mechanisms coincide: functional instability is 0.3972

Discovery does not return one mechanism under different descriptions: Cohen’s
kappa is 0.0146.

Random seeds are not the source: the seed selects the sampled prompts, i.e.

No claim is made about scale. One model, one task.

## 8 The filability protocol

Filability of an interpretability claim. For a filed claim $c$
derived from a circuit:

1.

Declare the specification space $\mathcal{S}$ : the analytic axes and the
levels of each that a competent analyst could defend, each with a citation.

2.

Declare the claim map $\varphi$ as deterministic, published code. Not a
language model.

3.

Compute $\pi^{*}=\max_{c}n_{c}/N$ over $\mathcal{S}$ , and $F$ by
Equation 2.

4.

The claim is filable at tolerance $\alpha$ if $\pi^{*}\geq 1-\alpha$ .

5.

Report $\pi^{*}$ , $F$ , the discard rate per axis level, and the
within-group decomposition of any pooled statistic.

A filing that cannot state its own $\pi^{*}$ has been asserted, not audited. The
regulator is not required to adjudicate among analytic choices; the filer declares
the space and reports the share that agrees.

## 9 Limitations

#### One model, one task.

Larger models have more components, widening both layer band and size class; the
sign of the effect on $F$ is unclear, and this limitation is the likeliest to move
the number.

A second-model replication is pre-registered but not run: a 924-cell grid on
Pythia-160m, a different architecture family performing the same task, identical
on every axis except a seed axis of three levels rather than five. Analysis plan,
reduced grid, and replication-versus-refutation criteria are committed and
timestamped before any cell ran; it will be reported in a revision in either
direction. A second task is designed and not run.

#### Circuit size is an outcome, not an axis.

Size is set by the threshold rule and has distorted three pooled quantities: $F$ ,
the direction of the null comparison, and the sign of the functional gap.
Conditioning on it drops $F$ from 0.7316 to 0.2746, more than standardising any
pre-registered axis. Every pooled statistic is reported with its within-size
decomposition.

#### The multiverse is as wide as the library, not the literature.

Optimal ablation [5] is defensible but not implemented by the instrument, so the
measured $F$ is a lower bound relative to the field’s full set of defensible
choices.

#### The discard rate is high and uneven.

52.3%, with a metric-imbalanced surviving pool. The threshold rule was fixed in
advance and no failing item repaired; the composition is stated, not adjusted.

#### The bootstrap is invalid for one reported family.

Where conditioning groups hold two to five specifications, retained self-pairs
dominate and intervals are unusable; those quantities are point estimates with the
diagnostic attached. No bias-corrected estimator was constructed post hoc.

#### On the instrument.

One of seven documented, publicly exported discovery objectives does not run on
the library’s canonical task, reported as a discard with its rate.

## 10 Discussion

#### What standardising one axis buys.

The metric removes 0.1377 of a 0.7316 flip rate; no single axis suffices.

#### On the instrument.

The failing objective bears on the maturity of the tooling on which regulatory
evidence would rest. Its authors are among those calling for the field to address
this [10].

#### What a regulator can take from this.

Evidentiary weight is a measurable property, and measuring it is cheap relative to
the sweep that produced the circuit.

## 11 Reproducibility

The pre-registration is a timestamped commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory
in the public repository, made before the confirmatory sweep. Every reported number
traces to a config, a seed and an environment fingerprint. The confirmatory sweep
ran under a single environment across all 1,320 cells, verified from the results
archive, and the code commit was recovered by content-addressed comparison of the
uploaded archive against the git tree, 22 of 22 files identical. The analysis layer
runs without a GPU.

A verification script recomputes every headline quantity from raw results: 36
checks, 0 failures, with $F$ derived by three routes including brute-force pairwise
computation. A second script checks every numeric token in the manuscript against
values derived from stored results. All tables are emitted directly from results.
The test suite is 343 tests.
